papers.title: A geospatial assessment of climate-induced hazards in the Papum Pare district of Arunachal Pradesh
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Abstract The Eastern Himalayas represent one of the world's most ecologically sensitive and dynamically evolving mountain systems, rendering them exceptionally vulnerable to contemporary climatic shifts. This study presents a comprehensive geospatial assessment of climate-induced hazards in the Papum Pare district of Arunachal Pradesh, India. Situated within the Sub-Himalayan and Lesser Himalayan zones, Papum Pare experiences extreme topographical variance, fragile geological formations and intensive monsoon regimes, culminating in acute susceptibility to flash floods, landslides and slope instability. Utilizing a multi-criteria evaluation (MCE) framework integrated within a Geographic Information System (GIS) and remote sensing environment, this research maps and analyzes hazard susceptibility across the district. Spatial parameters—including elevation, slope angle, slope aspect, lithology, soil characteristics, land use and land cover (LULC), normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) and proximity to drainage networks and road corridors—were parameterized, weighted using the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) and aggregated to generate district-wide hazard susceptibility indices. The empirical findings reveal that approximately 28% of the geographical area in Papum Pare falls under "High" to "Very High" hazard susceptibility categories, with urbanized expansion zones along river valleys and unengineered infrastructural arteries exhibiting the greatest risk profiles. The results underscore the imperative for localized climate adaptation strategies, risk-informed spatial planning and resilient infrastructure development in the Eastern Himalayan fringe. Keywords: Geospatial Assessment, Climate-Induced Hazards, Papum Pare, Arunachal Pradesh, Eastern Himalayas, Landslides, Flash Floods

papers.title: Lithostratigraphically-constrained landslide susceptibility modeling in red-bed basins using a bayesian probability-based mixture probabilistic neural network
papers.summary: Regional landslide susceptibility prediction commonly treats diverse failure mechanisms as a single statistical entity, an oversimplification that fails in lithologically complex red-bed basins, where retrogressive and translational landslides follow fundamentally distinct hydromechanical laws. Here we develop a mechanism-divergent framework that integrates frequency ratio factor screening, Bayesian probability for uncertainty-aware dataset construction, and a mixture probabilistic neural network to explicitly fuse multi-modal susceptibility indices. The approach is validated in Sanshui District, a subtropical red-bed basin in China, using a 15-year multi-source inventory. Random forest and logistic regression are coupled with frequency ratio and Bayesian strategies to independently predict each landslide type. Bayesian-enhanced models consistently outperform their frequency-ratio counterparts, with Bayesian random forest achieving the highest accuracy. The mixture probabilistic neural network captures spatial heterogeneity through distance-weighted neural connections, markedly improving regional mapping and attaining an area under the curve of 90.2%, substantially higher than the 66.7% of conventional unified models. Shapley additive explanation analysis identifies lithology, annual precipitation, and road proximity as dominant controls; lithostratigraphic Groups 1, 7, 12 and 13 exhibit the highest susceptibility. This framework offers a lithostratigraphy-informed, mechanism-aware pathway for landslide risk assessment in complex soft-rock terrains.

papers.summary: This research software snapshot documents the development of SOLUME Geotecnia Alerta, from the legacy V2.9 diagnostic model to V4.2 with a Zener solid and incremental constitutive memory. It includes preserved source code, archived outputs, newly reproduced results, an illustrated technical audit, and reproduction instructions. V2.9 regression summaries for a 55 mm/h reference run and a no-rain diagnostic were reproduced byte for byte. In the V4.2 reference rerun, the Direct Insertion Method (DIM) and an algebraically equivalent internal-variable update agree to a relative L2 difference of 7.27e-16 in final effective stress sigma_zz. A separate full-history constitutive comparison covers irregular strain increments, holds, and limiting decay factors, with relative L2 differences below 6.72e-16. These results verify the evaluation of the same discrete constitutive history. The package also reports two-level temporal and spatial sensitivity tests and a zero-rain control. Spatial refinement changes the peak viscoelastic memory by approximately 62% and activates surface saturation at some nodes. Spatial convergence, a complete global water budget, robust solver failure handling, independent coupled benchmarks, and field calibration remain open research tasks. Athy–Fernando is deliberately disabled in V4.2 to isolate the viscoelastic contribution; earlier AF experiments are retained as development history. All examples are synthetic. The software is an exploratory research prototype, and operational landslide-warning capability has not been demonstrated. Future development includes SOLUME Edge: reduced local computation, sensor integration, communication tests, and progressive laboratory and field evaluation. papers.title: Landslide Susceptibility Assessment in Badong County, Hubei Province, Based on Machine Learning and SHAP Interpretability Analysis
papers.summary: Badong County is located in the hinterland of the Three Gorges Reservoir Area and is characterized by complex geological conditions and highly rugged terrain, making landslide susceptibility assessment particularly important. Based on an inventory of 384 landslides, this study retained 11 conditioning factors and constructed a balanced dataset with a 1:1 ratio of landslide to non-landslide samples. Sensitivity analysis of 500, 1000, and 1500 m buffer distances showed only small differences in non-landslide sampling, with the 1000 m buffer retained for subsequent analysis. The dataset was evaluated using both a conventional 7:3 random training–test split and five-fold spatial block cross-validation, with the spatially independent results used as the primary basis for model evaluation. Four machine learning models, namely RF, MLP, SVM, and XGBoost, were compared. Under spatial block cross-validation, XGBoost achieved the highest mean AUC of 0.8662, compared with 0.8751 under the random split, and also showed the best overall performance among the four models. Calibration analysis further indicated good agreement between the predicted susceptibility scores and the observed landslide proportions. Bootstrap resampling was used to quantify prediction uncertainty, and the integration of susceptibility and uncertainty identified areas characterized by both high susceptibility and high uncertainty. Independent validation using spatially withheld landslides showed that the high- and very-high-susceptibility zones accounted for 29.25% of the study area and contained 71.61% of the withheld landslides. SHAP analysis indicated that elevation, distance to road, slope, and NDVI were the principal contributors to the XGBoost model output. Overall, the results provide a spatial reference for landslide susceptibility zoning, preliminary engineering-site screening, and the prioritization of field investigation and monitoring in Badong County.

papers.title: Cascading Cryosphere Hazards in a Warming Himalaya A Secondary-Data Analysis of the August 2026 Nepal–Tibet Glacier-Collapse Debris Flow
papers.source: International Journal of Sociology and Social Research
papers.summary: The glacier temporarily blocked the Lhende Khola River, then released a destructive debris flow that travelled through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli corridors into the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading in Nepal. This paper relies on secondary data from government disaster management bureaucracies and reporting from the United Nations, multilateral banks, and print and broadcast media. It focuses on the events surrounding the disaster, analysis of causal factors, casualties, damage to infrastructure and the economy, and response efforts by the government and international agencies. On August 29, 2026, the toll in Nepal was reported to be 675 dead with 2,478 missing and over 93,000 affected, while Tibet reported 7 dead and 560 missing persons. The calamity destroyed about 430 megawatts of hydropower capacity, 19 bridges, and 40 kilometres of road, while obliterating the vital Gyirong border crossing for Nepal-China trade. This paper discusses the event in the context of available scientific literature on glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) and ice–rock avalanches in High Mountain Asia, highlighting that the same Bhote Koshi corridor faced a similar transboundary glacial lake outburst event in 2016, which points to an issue of recurrent and unmitigated risk. The study finds there are still gaps in cross-border early detection, information sharing across borders, and infrastructure management based on climate risks, and gives some suggestions for governance and engineering. This study provides an early and organised description of a quickly changing disaster which will be useful for investigators, practitioners in civil defence planning, and policy-makers, but it also notes the limits of this investigation using secondary sources. papers.title: ResQNet: A Crowdsourced Disaster Preparedness and Real-Time SOS Mesh Network Using Wi-Fi Direct MANET, Delay Tolerant Networking, and Artificial Intelligence
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Natural disasters such as earthquakes, floods, cyclones, landslides, and wildfires frequently damage cellular towers and internet infrastructure, leaving victims unable to contact rescue teams and depriving responders of real-time situational information. This paper presents ResQNet, a crowdsourced, infrastructure-independent disaster communication system that uses Wi-Fi Direct-based Mobile Ad Hoc Networking (MANET) and Delay Tolerant Networking (DTN) to relay SOS alerts between nearby smartphones without relying on cellular or internet connectivity. Each smartphone in the network functions simultaneously as a sender, relay, and store-and-forward node: SOS packets, tagged with a unique identifier, timestamp, GPS coordinates, hop count, and time-to-live (TTL), are propagated hop by hop until they reach an internet-enabled gateway device or a rescue authority. Duplicate packet suppression and TTL-controlled flooding are used to keep the network efficient under heavy load. ResQNet further incorporates artificial intelligence for emergency severity classification, location-based clustering of victims, accessibility analysis, and hotspot identification, together with voice-triggered SOS activation for hands-free operation. A web-based dashboard visualizes live SOS alerts, victim clusters, and priority levels on a map to support rescue coordination. Simulation-based evaluation of packet delivery ratio, latency, and message loss indicates that the proposed architecture can sustain reliable emergency communication even when conventional networks fail, offering a scalable and low-cost foundation for future disaster-response systems.

Displacement at the ground surface was measured approximately daily (the time of record varied throughout the monitoring period) at locations upon the upper (E1), middle (E2), and lower (E3) parts of the landslide along its left lateral (southeastern) boundary using electronic cable extension transducers (extensometers; Celesco PT8101 model) with manufacturer-stated ±0.7 mm accuracy (extensometer_data.csv). Sensors and their anchors were installed above the ground surface on galvanized steel posts partly driven by hand into the ground on opposite sides of a strike-slip fault forming the landslide’s left margin. Posts were driven into the ground at angles such that the extension cable was oriented parallel to the fault and measured the length of cable extending from the sensor housing approximately parallel to the direction of landslide movement. Sensors had approximate maximum ranges of 1524 mm and were episodically reset to lower values by moving extension cables to newly driven anchor posts located closer to the sensors. However, sensors sometimes over-ranged and failed, likely providing inaccurate data when the maximum range was reached until failure occurred. Additional errors and omissions in the data likely resulted from problems with the solar- and battery-powered dataloggers including power loss, loading of rain, snow, and ice on extension cables and anchor posts, frost heaving, animal activity, and other factors. Erroneous data are excluded from the data provided here when that error was clear during inspection; however, it is almost certain that some error remains. papers.title: The Terra Nova Condominium: a critical evaluation of the population resettlement policy after the 2011 extreme-rainfall in nova Friburgo, Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil
papers.summary: This study examines the socio-spatial impacts of the Terra Nova Condominium, a housing complex in Nova Friburgo (RJ), established after the extreme rainfall-induced landslides and natural disaster of 2011. The relocation of displaced residents highlighted various vulnerabilities, exacerbated over time by inadequate planning and socio-spatial segregation. The findings reveal that prolonged residency in the complex correlates with greater dissatisfaction concerning building security and infrastructure. Additionally, the study identifies how the original community’s socio-cultural ties were severed, impeding adaptation. The residents, many from rural backgrounds, faced difficulties adjusting to urban life, missing their previous environments' social and economic benefits. This research parallels other global post-disaster resettlements, emphasizing the systemic flaws of top-down housing policies prioritizing profit over social needs, thereby intensifying the marginalization of vulnerable populations. The conclusion calls for more participatory approaches in housing policies, which include residents in decision-making processes, thus fostering resilience and reducing social vulnerability.

papers.title: Target-focused supervision and fine spatial evidence improve sparse landslide detection in remote-sensing imagery
papers.summary: Introduction Regional landslide screening must retrieve sparsely annotated failures among visually similar terrain while limiting false review candidates. Small scars can lose spatial detail during downsampling, and extensive background regions can dominate semantic supervision. Methods We developed the Sparse Landslide Detection Transformer (SLD-DETR) by adapting RT-DETRv4. It combines scale-guided focused distillation (SGFD), which concentrates teacher–student alignment near annotated landslides; high-resolution scale-aware supervision (HRSS), which supervises stride-4 features; and stride-4 decoder memory (S2-Mem), which exposes fine spatial features to query selection and cross-attention. We evaluated five independent training seeds on a source-scene-disjoint 6:2:2 split of the Multi-Scale Landslide Dataset (MSLD). For screening performance, confidence thresholds were calibrated on validation to a false-positive rate of no more than 0.10 false positives per image (FPPI), then frozen for testing. We also assessed zero-shot transfer to LRSTTC-New. Results On the held-out MSLD test split, SLD-DETR achieved a mean average precision of 58.07 ± 1.10 % across IoU thresholds 0.50–0.95 (mAP@50:95) and 63.43 ± 1.23 % mAP@75, compared with 53.90 ± 0.96 % and 58.34 ± 2.65 % , respectively, for RT-DETRv4-S. At the validation-calibrated operating points, test miss rate was 15.82 ± 2.18% for SLD-DETR and 18.63 ± 0.99% for the baseline. Under zero-shot cross-region transfer, all detectors degraded substantially; SLD-DETR had the highest AP within the RT-DETRv4 family, while RF-DETR-S performed best overall. Discussion The coordinated modules improved box-level screening on the evaluated source-disjoint MSLD split. SGFD and HRSS are training-only, whereas S2-Mem remains at inference and adds approximately 0.06 million parameters. Runtime and memory costs increase with image resolution.

Child health challenges in the 2025 Sumatra flood and landslide: Lessons for disaster risk reduction and emergency response
papers.source: Jàmbá Journal of Disaster Risk Studies
papers.summary: In late 2025, catastrophic floods and landslides struck Sumatra, Indonesia, causing widespread destruction and nearly 1200 fatalities. Children were among the most severely affected, experiencing acute health problems, disruptions in essential healthcare services and significant psychosocial distress. This essay employs an evidence-informed analytical approach, integrating contemporaneous official reports, available scientific literature, international disaster risk reduction (DRR) frameworks, Emergency Medical Team (EMT) standards and the authors’ direct field experience during the disaster response. The disaster is examined across the disaster management cycle, including prevention, mitigation, preparedness, emergency response and recovery, to identify gaps between established child-centred disaster management principles and their practical implementation. The analysis demonstrates that, despite national policies and international guidance, implementation was inconsistent. Many children experienced preventable illnesses, interruptions in chronic medical care, inadequate continuity of paediatric healthcare and unmet psychosocial needs because of coordination challenges, limited child-focused preparedness and fragmented service delivery. The findings highlight that integrating child-centred DRR principles with specialised paediatric emergency training, strengthened EMT deployment, continuity of essential child health services, coordinated mental health support and multisectoral collaboration can improve disaster preparedness and emergency response. The lessons learned provide practical guidance for strengthening child-centred DRR, improving emergency response systems and informing policy development that better integrates child protection and paediatric healthcare into all phases of disaster management.

papers.summary: The paper examines the main directions of the impact of natural hazards on the landscapes of Okriba and their role in the structural and functional transformation of landscapes. The study analyses the natural conditions of the territory, the spatial distribution patterns of hazardous processes, and their interrelationships with relief, geological structure, hydrological regime, soil, and vegetation cover. Particular attention is paid to landslides, erosion, debris flows, and flood processes, as well as to the potential impacts of extreme climatic events. One of the key areas of the research is the assessment of the interaction between natural hazards and anthropogenic pressures. The landscapes of Okriba are considered as geographical systems undergoing continuous transformation under the combined influence of natural and anthropogenic factors. The paper also assesses the vulnerability of different landscape types to natural hazards and identifies the main directions for enhancing their resilience. Based on the findings of the study, several characteristic landscape settings were identified as particularly susceptible to the development and spatial occurrence of landslide processes. These include river-valley slopes; highly dissected hilly and low-mountain terrain; slopes adjacent to transportation infrastructure, particularly roads; and anthropogenically modified slopes in the vicinity of settlements. The results of the study can be applied to the rational use of Okriba’s natural resources, spatial planning, environmental management, and the development of measures aimed at reducing natural hazard risks.

papers.title: LIA-adaptive Goldstein phase filtering for improved InSAR displacement estimation in landslide-prone terrain
papers.summary: Abstract Reliable InSAR-based monitoring of ground deformation is often hindered by atmospheric disturbances and phase noise, particularly in regions with rugged topography and high vegetation cover. However, limited work has explored integrated phase filtering and atmospheric correction strategies in complex, landslide-prone terrains like Mizoram, India. This study proposes an enhanced methodology combining a Modified Goldstein phase filter and Atmospheric Phase Screen (APS) removal to improve Line of Sight (LOS) displacement estimation. Mizoram, characterized by frequent landslides and challenging climatic conditions, provides an ideal testbed to evaluate these improvements. Twenty Sentinel-1 SAR images (10 ascending, 10 descending) were processed using SRTM DEM-based co-registration, with corrections addressing height distortions and DEM voids. This study modifies the standard Goldstein filter that incorporates Local Incidence Angle (LIA) information to enhance phase unwrapping stability, combined with Atmospheric Phase Screen (APS) removal applied before phase filtering. Furthermore, an ensemble learning framework using a Random Forest regressor was employed to model and refine time-series displacement trends. The proposed method constrained phase values within a range of -3 to 3 radians, improved displacement map interpretability, and achieved a LOS displacement of±80 mm/month. Validation against ground-collected levelling survey data showed a strong correlation of 76% (n=20 levelling points, p < 0.01) with the modified Goldstein filter applied LOS displacement values, as against 46% (n=20 levelling points, p < 0.05) for the normal Goldstein phase filter applied LOS values. Additionally, 5-fold cross-validation of the Random Forest ensemble model yielded training and testing R² values of 0.892 and 0.856, respectively, confirming the reliability of the displacement estimates.

papers.title: SBAS InSAR, UAV, and Numerical Modeling of Slope Instability in Tbilisi, Georgia
papers.summary: The Vere River basin in Tbilisi, Georgia, experienced a major cascading landslide–flood disaster in June 2015, emphasizing the need to evaluate the present stability of slopes adjacent to the former source area. This study combines small-baseline InSAR (SBAS), RTK-UAV photogrammetry, COSI-Corr image correlation and LS-RAPID numerical modeling to investigate whether the slope remains active and how it responds to changing pore-pressure conditions. Analysis of 109 ascending Sentinel-1 acquisitions acquired between April 2022 and October 2025 revealed persistent positive line-of-sight deformation across the investigated slope. Independent UAV/COSI-Corr analysis identified horizontal displacements of approximately 0.05–0.09 m over 149 days, exceeding the empirical relative displacement detection threshold of 0.0235 m. The measured displacement direction broadly follows the downslope and structural orientation, although its angular offset suggests that the movement is influenced by a combination of topography, bedding, fractures, and heterogeneous slope materials rather than a single planar control. LS-RAPID simulations further showed a nonlinear response to increasing prescribed pore-pressure ratio. Together, the observations indicate that the slope has not fully stabilized after the 2015 event and continues to undergo slow deformation while remaining sensitive to hydrological conditions. This is particularly important for Tbilisi because renewed slope instability in the Vere valley could interact with the confined river corridor and urban infrastructure, increasing the potential for cascading impacts.

papers.title: Extreme Rainfall-Induced Landslides on 1 June 2025 in Southern Assam, Northeast India
papers.source: Journal of the Geological Society of India
papers.summary: ABSTRACT In the early hours of 1 June 2025, a series of landslides occurred in the Rajpur Village of southern Assam, Northeast India, following incessant rainfall due to early onset of the Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM). The landslides occurred almost simultaneously along the partially weathered hillslopes composed primarily of matrix supported gravels, between 03:00 and 03:30 IST. These were preceded by an extreme rainfall pulse of 230 mm recorded at 02:30 IST which is part of a cumulative total of 458.8 mm over the previous three days in the area. The landsides caused grievous injuries to a few people and damaged number of dwelling units with consequent displacements. Post disaster site investigation and first-hand accounts suggest an extreme rainfall triggered shallow landslide mechanism in play when saturation in the porous rock and soil mass exceeded threshold. In this report we present a preliminary assessment of the rainfall event and physical site factors leading to the landslides on this particular date. The good correlation observed here between rainfall record and occurrence of landslides provides an important case study to work out a regional threshold for rainfall triggered landslides in the foreland fold belt region of Northeast India. This will further contribute towards developing a region-specific landslide early warning system in a scenario of changing monsoonal regime.

papers.title: Safety and Resilience in Slope Engineering Design for New Buildings under Extreme Rainstorm Climates
papers.summary: The safety of construction slopes holds significant importance in engineering and architecture, with the lack of resilience against extreme weather conditions being particularly critical. This paper systematically examines the fundamental flaws in traditional design theories regarding the limitations of compression-shear stress paths and the assumption of constant soil parameters. It delves into the systemic vulnerabilities in resilience across the entire lifecycle caused by operational supervision gaps and post-event regulatory gaps in the current construction system. Additionally, it reveals the consequences of mechanistic isolation between structural support and ecological protection, as well as the oversimplified engineering approach resulting from outdated drainage system standards, through real-world disaster case studies. Based on this, this article proposes a theoretical revision direction for constructing a tension shear fluid-solid coupling unsaturated soil mechanics system, explores a differentiated zoning control mechanism based on quantitative risk analysis (QRA), and integrates digital Bayesian pre-evaluation methods with on-site observations. The research aims to provide rigorous theoretical support for the disaster-resistant design of high-risk building slope engineering, and promote the transformation of slope engineering from static defense to a dynamic resilience management paradigm throughout its lifecycle.

papers.title: Integrating rockfall and debris flow monitoring and early warning networks into risk mitigation and emergency planning in Brescia Province, Italy
papers.summary: Italy is highly exposed to rapid landslides such as rockfalls and debris flows, which strongly affect mountain communities, infrastructure, and land management. Mitigation strategies traditionally rely on structural measures, including active stabilization works and passive protection systems, but their effectiveness depends on site-specific geological and geomorphological conditions and event magnitude. In this context, monitoring and Early Warning Systems are increasingly recognized as essential tools to complement structural interventions and reduce loss of life. Recent advances in sensors, communication technologies, and data processing have made local and territorial landslide Early Warning Systems more feasible, although their implementation remains challenging due to false alarms, threshold definition, validation procedures, and the need for continuous maintenance. This paper presents three case studies from the Province of Brescia, Northern Italy, showing how monitoring and alarm systems can be integrated into risk mitigation and land management. The first concerns a rockfall-prone site where unusual trajectories and high bounce heights required a combined system of flexible barriers, a multipurpose interception net, impact sensors, and traffic-light-based warning devices. The second describes a debris-flow Early Warning Network based on continuous meteorological and hydrometric monitoring, event-triggered wire sensors, and rainfall thresholds. The third illustrates an integrated multi-hazard network that monitors rockfalls, debris flows, and floods at the municipal scale. Together, the case studies highlight the value of combining structural and non-structural measures to support emergency planning and improve territorial safety.

papers.source: Journal of Environmental Engineering and Landscape Management
papers.summary: Landslide is a frequent form of natural disaster in a tropical region such as Western Sarawak, Malaysia, and the occurrences are commonly associated with the wet season. Contemporarily, Landslide Susceptibility Map (LSM) produced by machine learning models are used to assess the landslide risk. However, LSMs are known to have spatiotemporal issues, where recent changes in the spatial data used as inputs in the models are not reflected in the LSMs, causing unjustified landslide susceptibility score in certain areas. The same issue was also observed in Western Sarawak’s LSM. Thus, this study was focused on transforming the Artificial Neural Network model used developed the region’s LSM into a set of equations that can be used as a landslide risk assessment system. The new system was determined to be highly accurate with a score of 1 for both Area Under the Curve score, and recall.

papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: EarthTrends is a multi-source Earth Observation framework developed to assess the impact of permafrost thaw on land degradation across the Arctic. Rapid warming is accelerating processes such as thermokarst formation, vegetation change, slope instability, and risks to infrastructure, yet monitoring these dynamics requires integrating heterogeneous satellite datasets and analytical methods. EarthTrends addresses this challenge through a modular Python architecture that fuses long-term satellite archives (Landsat), Copernicus Sentinel data, MODIS time series, and high-resolution optical imagery with advanced statistical and artificial intelligence approaches. The framework quantifies ecosystem change using multi-sensor vegetation index time series analysed through linear regression, Mann–Kendall trend tests, and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models to detect non-linear dynamics and anomalies. Thermokarst features are automatically mapped from high-resolution imagery using a U-Net deep learning segmentation model. Land degradation susceptibility is further evaluated by modelling soil freeze–thaw cycles as proxies for slope instability and landslide potential. Environmental indicators are intersected with socio-economic datasets to estimate impacts on settlements and infrastructure. Preliminary results show that the thermokarst detection component is operational and capable of identifying surface subsidence features, while freeze–thaw analyses reveal anomalies linked to areas of increased degradation risk. Vegetation trends highlight spatially heterogeneous ecosystem responses to warming across the Arctic. Overall, EarthTrends demonstrates the feasibility of an integrated, scalable framework for monitoring permafrost-driven environmental change and its societal implications. The system is intended for pan-Arctic application and will be released as an open-source tool to support research, monitoring, and decision-making related to climate-induced land degradation.

papers.title: Failure mechanism and dynamic process of the Jinping high-position and long-runout landslide in the Wumeng mountainous area, China, on 8th February 2025
papers.summary: The Wumeng Mountain area is characterized by complex geological conditions and is prone to high-position, long-runout landslide–debris flow chains. This study integrates field investigation, remote sensing interpretation, InSAR monitoring, laboratory tests, and numerical simulation to reveal the deformation evolution, genetic mechanism, and kinematic process of the landslide. The results show that the controlling factors can be stratified into two levels. At the geological level, the anti-dip fragmented rock mass with interbedded hard and soft strata constitutes the primary internal cause of slope instability, while the steep-upper and gentle-lower topography provides the morphological precondition for the transformation of the sliding mass into a debris flow. At the rainfall level, continuous infiltration significantly reduces slope stability and acts as the key triggering factor. Initial deformation appeared in 2014 and accelerated continuously after 2020, eventually leading to failure, with unstable rock masses still remaining at the rear scarp. Simulation results show that the entire process lasts about 50 s, with a maximum velocity of 48 m/s and a maximum accumulation thickness of 23 m, accompanied by progressive fragmentation of the rock mass. Such landslides share similar disaster-prone characteristics, which can provide references for the early identification of potential landslide hazards in the region.

papers.title: Water service disruption and emergency restoration following the 2026 Kumamoto earthquake
GIS-based assessment of population and dwelling exposure to landslide-prone areas in the Valencian Community (Spain)
papers.summary: The spatial identification of population exposure to landslide-prone areas is essential for risk-informed territorial planning, particularly where impacts affect peri-urban and dispersed residential areas rather than consolidated urban centres. This study presents a GIS-based, multi-scale methodology to quantify and locate population and dwelling exposure beyond administrative boundaries by integrating landslide susceptibility mapping, residential cadastral data, and high-resolution population information from the 2021 census grid. Exposure is assessed by combining residential cadastral parcels with high- and very-high-susceptibility zones and aggregating exposed parcels into Residential Clusters at Risk (RCr). Exposure values are classified using Tail Quantiles Breaks (TQB) based on the P50, P70, P85, and P95 percentiles, providing a classification scheme well suited to heavy-tailed population distributions. Application to the Valencian Community (Spain) shows that population exposure is low at the regional scale (approximately 0.25% of the total population) but spatially uneven. Inland areas exhibit higher exposure intensity associated with permanent residential settlements, whereas coastal tourist-oriented areas concentrate higher absolute exposure linked to extensive built-up areas. Sensitivity analyses confirm the robustness of the methodology across aggregation radii and classification thresholds. The proposed methodology supports territorial planning and preventive interventions but represents an exposure assessment rather than a complete landslide risk analysis.

papers.title: Monitoring in Open-Pit Mines
papers.summary: Open-pit mining creates large, evolving excavations with high rock slopes, variable hydrogeological conditions, and continuous disturbance from blasting and excavation. These factors make slope instability a persistent operational risk and a major safety hazard. Modern open-pit geotechnical monitoring has therefore shifted from periodic, manual measurements to integrated, near-real-time systems that combine surface and subsurface sensors, ground-based radar, laser scanning, UAV photogrammetry, and satellite InSAR. In Mining 4.0, these sensing technologies are increasingly connected through IoT-enabled data acquisition, automated quality control, analytics pipelines, and decision-support tools, including digital twins and trigger-action response plans (TARPs), to provide timely warnings, reduce exposure to hazardous ground movement, and support production continuity. This chapter presents a practical framework for designing and operating slope monitoring programs in open pits, linking failure mechanisms to monitoring objectives, instrument selection, data management, alarm philosophy, and operational response. Several case studies illustrate how multi-source monitoring improves hazard recognition, forecasting, and risk-based decision-making, including the 2013 Manefay landslides at Bingham Canyon Mine and operational examples of radar, prism, UAV, and InSAR integration.

papers.title: GIS-based spatial prioritization of natural-hazard exposure and recorded COVID-19 case counts in Lemery, Batangas, Philippines
papers.summary: Local governments often maintain separate natural-hazard maps and health-surveillance records but lack a transparent method for identifying areas where these concerns overlap. This study applied a Geographic Information System (GIS) sieve-mapping approach to prioritize the 46 barangays of Lemery, Batangas, Philippines using 2,505 confirmed COVID-19 cases and ten natural-hazard layers covering seismic, landslide, coastal, flood, and volcanic hazards. QGIS was used to convert hazard classes into ordinal scores, adjust scores according to the proportion of barangay area affected, apply predefined weights, and generate a composite ranking. The decision premise was that barangays with high absolute COVID-19 case counts and substantial mapped hazard exposure may warrant greater preparedness priority. A balanced 50/50 weighting between the health and natural-hazard domains was used as an a priori screening scenario, not as evidence of equal contributions to disaster loss. Natural-hazard weights reflected qualitative local frequency information rather than probabilistic loss estimates. The additive combining rule summed the scaled health component and weighted, area-adjusted hazard scores without modelling interactions or joint probabilities. Bukal recorded the highest absolute number of confirmed COVID-19 cases, while District IV, Wawa Ibaba, Palanas, Mataas Na Bayan, and Sambal Ilaya received the five highest composite priority scores. The resulting ranking represents relative planning priority rather than infection risk or probabilistic disaster risk. Future work should incorporate population normalization, sensitivity analysis, vulnerability and exposure indicators, hazard interactions, and finer-resolution data.

papers.title: Flood and Landslide Risks in Border Regions
papers.summary: The increasing frequency of hydrometeorological disasters in border regions reflects the interaction between environmental degradation, land-use change, and climate variability. Nunukan Regency, as a strategic border area of Indonesia, faces significant development pressure due to the conversion of forests and agricultural land into plantations and settlements. This study examines how environmental degradation contributes to rising disaster risks and its relevance to spatial planning policy design. It focuses on the roles of land-use change and rainfall in shaping the spatial distribution of flood and landslide risks and their integration into the 2024–2043 Regional Spatial Plan (RTRW). Using a qualitative descriptive approach based on secondary data, the findings show that upstream land cover changes increase runoff and intensify flood risks downstream, while vegetation loss in hilly areas elevates landslide risks. Although the RTRW has incorporated disaster mitigation conceptually, gaps remain in aligning policy design with land-use control.

papers.title: Implementing a climate-resilient and inclusive WASH guidance in Indonesia: A mixed-methods case study.
papers.summary: Climate change increasingly disrupts water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services, disproportionately affecting women, children, people with disabilities, and groups with limited adaptive resources. Evidence remains limited on how WASH programs integrate climate resilience, equity, and social inclusion and on the conditions that enable benefits to reach households. Researchers examined how Climate Change Response for Inclusive WASH (CCRIW) guidance was implemented and adapted within routine programming in Indonesia, how implementation outcomes related to post-implementation household access, and which contextual factors enabled or constrained such access. Researchers conducted a mixed-methods study using program data collected between August 2023 and October 2024. Data included key informant interviews (n = 29) and a group discussion (n = 10). Quantitative data included village workshop records (n = 91) and household surveys and observations (n = 1,243) from 12 villages affected by floods, landslides, and drought. Researchers used descriptive statistics and logistic regression and triangulated the findings with deductive qualitative analysis informed by an implementation science framework. Results indicated that CCRIW guidance was perceived as relevant but was adapted during implementation rather than adopted as a complete stand-alone protocol. These adaptations appeared to improve short-term practicality while reducing consistent application, depth of learning, and recall of CCRIW as a distinct approach. Communities primarily adopted lower-cost actions aligned with immediate needs, available resources, and perceived feasibility. Household modifications supported more resilient and inclusive access but could not replace system-level investments under severe hazards. Regression models showed district-level associations for several facility-specific outcomes, limited associations with multiple-hazard exposure, and no consistent associations with reported household c

papers.title: Determination of the damage range in the toe zone of gentle piedmont slopes based on hydraulic mechanisms
papers.summary: This study presents a novel hydro-mechanical framework for assessing damage development in the toe zone of gentle piedmont slopes by integrating seepage analysis and beam theory. SEEP3D numerical simulations are performed to characterise pore-water pressure and confined water distributions under variable slope geometries, dimensions of water-blocking structures, and rainfall characteristics. Based on confined water distribution, the slope toe region is classified into two distinct zones. Zone A, featuring a triangular uplift pressure distribution, is analysed using a simply supported beam model, whereas Zone B, with a trapezoidal uplift pressure distribution, is idealised as a cantilever beam. The results reveal that slope length and the embedded depth of water-blocking structures exert the most significant control over seepage characteristics. Rainfall duration and intensity also govern confined water distribution, with V-shaped and incremental rainfall patterns exerting the most prominent impacts on seepage fields. Deformation and cracking behaviours within both zones are systematically investigated to quantify damage extent at the slope toe. The combined numerical simulation and mechanical modelling approach established herein provides a quantitative and mechanistic tool for evaluating slope stability and supporting landslide mitigation in gentle piedmont areas.

papers.title: Hydrological dynamics and morphological physiognomies of Dzüdza River, Nagaland, India: A Geographical Information System‐based quantification of drainage morphometry
papers.summary: Abstract The assessment of the morphometric characteristics of the Dzüdza River basin in Nagaland has been critically important for hydrological analysis, flood risk assessment, soil erosion evaluation, and sustainable regional development, owing to its strategic location on the northern fringes of the Himalayas and flanked by hills to the east. In this mountainous region, the topographical changes with the growing impacts of climate change can significantly impact the river systems and intensify the occurrence of extreme hydrological events. The objective of the present research work is to quantify the drainage morphometry using geoprocessing techniques. The 30 m spatial resolution Cartosat Digital Elevation Model (DEM) was analyzed in ArcGIS environment to delineate the sub‐catchments/catchments and extract the stream networks. Nine sub‐catchments (SC 1–SC 9) and a main catchment (MC) were delineated to assess the morphometric parameters. The following morphometric aspects are derived: drainage network analysis, basin geometry, drainage texture, and relief characteristics. Two prominent drainage patterns, that is, dendritic and trellis patterns, are identified. Most of the parameters analyzed have indicated SCs (3, 5, and 8) with higher mean discharge, mean annual runoff, higher peak flow for shorter periods of time and high runoff, consequently, making it vulnerable to flash floods. However, SCs (1, 2, 7, and 9) are predicted to exhibit higher susceptibility to sheet erosion. The relief characteristics suggest a rugged as well as highly dissected landscape with the presence of steep slopes and strong relief. The hypsometric integral (0.46) indicates that erosional progress is at an equilibrium stage. The use of Cartosat DEM and Geographical Information System application has proven its efficiency and reliability in the assessment of morphometric parameters of Dzüdza River and comprehending the hydrological dynamics and morphological physiognomies. papers.title: Morphological characteristics and spatial distribution of shallow landslides in the Qinling-Daba Mountains, China
papers.summary: Shallow landslides dominate the hazard inventory of the Qinba Mountains, China, yet their regional-scale characteristics and controlling factors remain poorly understood. Based on 4,315 historical shallow landslides (1998–2022), this study integrates field measurements, GIS-based spatial analysis, and statistical methods to investigate landslide morphology, spatial distribution, and conditioning factors. Methodologically, we used variable-specific correlation analyses (Spearman, Cramér’s V , Kruskal–Wallis H tests) and multi-buffer processing for linear features (faults, rivers, roads). Results reveal: (1) Power law scaling in area-volume ( V = 2.27 A 1.034 ) and size-frequency distribution (exponent 2.27), confirming self-organized criticality of the landslide system. (2) Regional differentiation: the Hanjiang River basin shows a gradient from high-density, small failures upstream to lower-density, larger failures downstream; the Jialingjiang and the Hanjiang tributary basins are dominated by larger landslides due to competent lithologies and higher relief. (3) Key controlling factors: epimetamorphic rocks, elevation 10 persons/km 2 , and distance to roads (<500 m), rivers (<1,800 m) and faults (<6,000 m). In general, macro-topography, regional tectonics, and climate collaboratively define the potential locations of landslides, whereas micro-topography, lithology, and vegetation cover govern their scale and type; Human activities change the dominant geometry of landslides to a certain extent. (4) The spatial pattern of landslide in continuous variables is analyzed at a 36 km distance threshold, with mean annual precipitation exhibiting the strongest positive spatial autocorrelation (Moran’s I = 0.93), and LISA maps show High-High clusters of precipitation and coefficient of elevation variation in Ankang, while elevation shows an opposite pattern. papers.title: Contrasting drivers of summer extreme hourly precipitation over the southeastern and northeastern Tibetan Plateau
papers.summary: Abstract Extreme hourly precipitation (EHP) across the Tibetan Plateau (TP) often triggers flash floods and landslides due to the region's complex and steep terrain, yet its inter-station covariations and formation mechanisms remain inadequately understood. Using climate network analysis of hourly station data and dynamic diagnostics, this study examines EHP synchronicity across the southeastern and northeastern TP and elucidates the underlying mechanisms from a perspective of sea surface temperature (SST)-forced circulation evolution. Results show weak inter-regional synchronization of EHP occurrence between the southeastern and northeastern TP, along with an insignificant correlation in EHP frequency (EHPF) between the two subregions, indicating largely independent governing physical processes. The southeastern TP EHPF is controlled by an upper-tropospheric South Asian anticyclone and a low-level anticyclone over the Arabian Sea. The South Asian anticyclone weakens after 2000, accompanied by intensified cyclonic circulation over the northern TP. In contrast, the northeastern TP EHPF is dominated by a quasi-barotropic Northeast Asian anticyclone throughout the entire period. SST drivers of EHPF over these two subregions exhibit both regional differences and interdecadal shifts. During 1979–1999, southeastern TP EHPF is linked to an eastern North Atlantic tripole SST anomaly pattern through a teleconnection wave train, whereas northeastern TP EHPF correlates with a western North Atlantic tripole configuration. After 2000, Eurasian Arctic SST anomalies emerge as dominant signals—a dipole pattern for the southeastern TP and a uniform warming pattern for the northeastern TP. These results underscore the need for region-specific EHP analysis and prediction strategies and highlight the growing role of the Arctic.

papers.title: Analysis on deformation and failure of multi-stage high slopes in open-pit mines based on strength reduction method
papers.summary: Multi-stage high slopes in open-pit mines containing weak diabase dikes exhibit complex progressive stepwise sliding failure under the combined effects of excavation disturbance and rainfall, yet their staged instability evolution laws remain insufficiently clarified in existing research. Taking the No.1 high slope of the Maoniup Rare Earth Mine in western Sichuan as the research object, this study systematically reveals the deformation-failure mechanism controlled by diabase weak interlayers through field geological investigation, in-situ shear tests and FLAC3D strength reduction numerical simulation. Field surveys show that the slope develops numerous tensile cracks on multi-level platforms and local slumping between platforms, with fractured, water-sensitive diabase dikes serving as the dominant internal weak structural planes triggering instability; Monitoring data show a progressive-failure pattern propagating from the 3,056 m platform toward the 3,080 m platform; in-situ shear test results confirm that diabase possesses extremely low saturated shear strength, which deteriorates sharply after rainwater softening. A three-dimensional numerical model matching actual stratigraphy and platform topography is established, and the Mohr–Coulomb strength reduction method is adopted to reproduce the whole progressive failure process under continuous strength degradation. The simulation results indicate that deformation initiates at diabase outcrops on the upper 3,056 m platform, and shear strain bands and plastic failure zones gradually extend downward along diabase belts to form interconnected through-going slip surfaces across multi-stage platforms, which well reproduces the field stepwise sliding characteristics. Numerical calculations using saturated geomechanical parameters under rainfall conditions yield a slope safety factor of 1.15, and the resultant deformation-failure pattern is highly consistent with simulation results obtained with strength reduction factors

papers.title: Residual shear strength of tropical granitic soils in Peninsular Malaysia
papers.summary: Introduction: Residual shear strength is an important parameter in the assessment of long-term slope stability and reactivated landslides. However, limited information is available on the residual shear strength behaviour of tropical granitic residual soils in Malaysia. This study investigated the residual shear strength characteristics of granitic residual soils collected from three locations in the northern region of Peninsular Malaysia: Kulim Hi-Tech, Bukit Suling, and Bukit Katak. Materials and methods: Laboratory characterisations encompassed physical index testing, particle density determination, mechanical sieve–hydrometer analyses, and Multiple-Reversal Direct Shear Testing (MR-DST) conducted under fully drained, saturated conditions across effective normal stresses of 50 kPa, 100 kPa, and 150 kPa. Results: The results indicated that residual shear behaviour was predominantly friction-controlled, with adopted effective residual friction angles ranging from 18.9° to 23.5°. Regression analysis revealed strong negative linear trends between effective residual friction angle and soil index properties (plasticity index (PI), liquid limit (LL), and clay fraction (CF)). However, because these relationships were derived from three site-level observations ( n = 3) without external validation, they are presented strictly as preliminary site-specific empirical correlations and must not be interpreted as design-ready predictive tools. Conclusions: This study expands the limited database for tropical granitic residual soils in Malaysia, demonstrating that index properties provide practical preliminary screening guidance while highlighting that direct, site-specific laboratory testing remains indispensable for final geotechnical design.

papers.title: Refinement of the Burridge and Knopoff Resistance Function with the Elementary Catastrophe Theory
papers.summary: The soil liquefaction occurs in water-saturated soils, involving a phase transition from solid to fluid when the soil loses strength and stiffness due to some change in its stress conditions. In physics, processes of this type are modeled according to the “fold” elementary catastrophe (for example, the over-saturated vapor condensation as well as some electromagnetism phenomena). Unlike our case, the respective graphs representing the aforementioned phenomena were obtained before the emergence of the Elementary Catastrophe Theory, which therein only clarified the processes and suggested some applications. In our circumstances, the behavior of the soil resistance at low speeds was not known. Consequently, after an appropriate application of the “fold” catastrophe, it was provided the resistance law at low speeds. All of the above would allow through the reengineering methods obtaining valuable information related to the structure and behavior of local plates. With this, we dared to suppose that in view of future landslide models already there is available a “standard” basic description that we believe is essential to be included at the time of any further development.

papers.title: Edukasi dan Sosialisasi Kebencanaan Longsor Berbasis Komunitas untuk Penguatan Kelembagaan Komunitas Peduli Lingkungan Kampung Asbaken
papers.summary: Kampung Asbaken in Distrik Makbon, Kabupaten Sorong, faces recurring landslide risks due to steep topography, high rainfall, uncontrolled land clearing, and sparse deep-rooted vegetation. Compounding this vulnerability, local disaster literacy is limited, and the partner group, Komunitas Peduli Lingkungan Kampung Asbaken, lacks formal organizational structures and standard operating procedures (SOPs). This community engagement initiative aimed to enhance community-based landslide mitigation and strengthen local institutional capacity through training, participatory risk mapping, slope bioengineering, and evacuation-route marking. Involving 25 partner members and 30 residents across three workshops, the program evaluated knowledge gains using a 30-item pretest-posttest instrument. The mean knowledge score increased by 78.6%, rising from 48.7 (SD = 9.8) to 87.0 (SD = 6.9), while passing rates (score ≥ 70) improved from 20.0% to 90.0% (paired t = 17.4, p < .001). The partner group also formalized its organizational structure and mitigation SOPs. These results show that participatory education integrated with vegetative conservation and institutional capacity building effectively enhances rural disaster resilience.

An AI-Based Early Warning Framework for Natural Disasters in Afghanistan
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Afghanistan gets hit by floods, earthquakes, landslides, droughts and avalanches, sometimes all in one year, sometimes in the same valley. In remote mountain villages the damage gets worse for a simple reason: the warning shows up late, or it never shows up. This paper sketches an early warning system built around Afghan conditions, with AI handling the data work. It would pull in weather readings, past disaster records, satellite images and terrain data, then estimate how likely each hazard is and sort that into four risk levels. Warnings would go out by SMS, radio, mobile apps and local community networks, but only after a real person has checked them.To be upfront, this is a proposal and nothing is running yet. Earthquakes can't be predicted, so for those the aim is risk maps and faster alerts once one has started. The idea is to back up the official disaster-management agencies and leave the final calls with them.

papers.title: Progressive deformation and reinforcement control of a mountain slope under sequential excavation of multiple underground openings
papers.summary: Sequential excavation of multiple underground openings in steep slopes can reactivate previously disturbed ground and adversely affect tunnel support and slope stability. This study investigates disturbance-zone evolution and reinforcement effects in a mountain slope containing two tunnel anchorages and a main tunnel. A three-dimensional finite difference model was developed to simulate anchorage excavation followed by main tunnel excavation. The simulated displacement trends were generally consistent with the measured trends. Seven numerical cases were compared in terms of deformation, shear localization, primary-support safety, and global slope stability. The results indicate that anchorage excavation generated localized shear deformation and yielded zones, which underwent further deformation during main tunnel excavation, with increased connectivity of shear deformation and plastic yielding among the openings and toward the slope surface. Compared with conventional support, integrated tunnel reinforcement reduced the maximum system displacement from 94.2 to 40.3 mm (57.2%) and increased the minimum primary-support safety factor from 0.61 to 1.10. For the reinforcement arrangement examined, omitting prestressed bolts caused the greatest deterioration among the component-omission cases, increasing the peak displacement at tunnel monitoring points from approximately 39 to 46 mm and reducing the minimum support safety factor to 0.98. Adding the field-designed left- and right-side anti-slide pile configurations increased the global slope safety factor from 1.20 to 1.32 and 1.28, respectively. Among these configurations, the left-side piles more effectively reduced the continuity of the potential shear-deformation pathway toward the lower slope surface. papers.title: Nepal Landslide Dam Catalog (NLDC): An inventory of valley-blocking landslides in Nepal compiled through 2020
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: The Nepal Landslide Dam Catalog (NLDC) is an inventory of valley-blocking landslides in Nepal compiled in 2020. It includes landslides that reached a river channel and fully blocked, partially blocked, or substantially narrowed it. Following Costa & Schuster (1988), we refer to all of these as landslide dams. A lake was confirmed behind only some events, and some landslides may never have completely blocked the river. Landslide dams are an important hazard in Nepal. They can inundate land upstream and, if the dam fails, generate sudden downstream floods and debris flows. Events such as the 2014 Jure landslide dam on the Sunkoshi River and the 2015 Ramche landslide dam on the Kali Gandaki illustrate these risks. Before NLDC, information on landslide dams in Nepal was dispersed across news reports, global inventories, national disaster records, and studies of individual events. NLDC consolidates these records into a documented, openly available dataset. The catalog contains 240 mapped landslide dams identified and located using satellite imagery. Of these, 128 formed between 2000 and 2020, 78 were triggered by the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, and 34 are older or have uncertain dates. Landslide polygons are available for 208 events. Two supplementary tables provide records of 32 additional landslide dams reported in previous publications and event timelines for six well-documented cases. papers.title: Al-Mīzān Conceptual Framework for Ecological Mitigation: A Thematic Exegesis of Qur’anic Responses to Hydrometeorological Crises
papers.summary: The hydrometeorological crisis in Indonesia, marked by the catastrophic flash floods and landslides that struck Sumatra and Aceh in late 2025, has been demonstrated to originate primarily from large-scale deforestation and upstream land-use conversion rather than from extreme rainfall anomalies alone. Although disaster mitigation studies in Southeast Asia have advanced substantially in their technical, infrastructural, and institutional dimensions, the spiritual and religious values that motivate community behavior toward ecosystems remain largely overlooked. Likewise, existing studies on Islamic ecotheology have yet to be operationalized into a systematic disaster mitigation framework. This study aims to identify and synthesize the hermeneutical clusters derived from the Qur’an that constitute the al-mīzān conceptual framework, examine their conceptual relevance to the causal roots of the 2025 Sumatra–Aceh disaster, and formulate their operational implications for strengthening value-based disaster mitigation. papers.title: Indiana's Landslides—Exploring Their Causes, Features, and Distribution: StoryMap, database, and photo gallery
papers.summary: Landslides occur throughout Indiana and are common in the hilly landscapes of southern Indiana, where identifying their distribution is important for understanding geologic hazards and supporting infrastructure and land-use planning. Understanding where landslides have occurred and where they may occur is important for protecting communities, infrastructure, and the environment. This project includes a StoryMap explaining landslide development and detection, and a geodatabase and photo gallery of mapped features in south-central Indiana. Landslide areas were delineated as polygon features primarily through interpretation of statewide Quality Level 2 (QL2) lidar data, supplemented by targeted field verification. The project focuses on the USGS Bedford, Jasper, and Tell City 1:100,000-scale quadrangles and expands previous landslide inventory mapping toward seamless coverage of southern Indiana. Data were integrated into the Indiana Geological and Water Survey landslide inventory to improve publicly accessible information on landslide locations and characteristics and to support hazard assessment, emergency preparedness, infrastructure planning, and landslide risk management.

papers.title: Mass movements in the southern Black Forest, Germany
papers.summary: Despite their importance as geomorphological processes and natural hazards, systematic inventories of mass movements remain limited for many Central European mid-mountain ranges. This study presents an inventory map of mass movements in the southern Black Forest (Germany), on the area of the Late Pleistocene Feldberg glaciation. High-resolution digital elevation models combined with field surveys were used to map and classify mass movements. Potential preconditioning factors (aspect, slope angle, lithology) were analysed. In total, 158 mass movements were identified, affecting 36.2 km² (6%) of the study area. Slides dominate the inventory (36%). The spatial distribution reveals two clusters with higher frequencies, larger sizes and greater vertical extent of mass movements. Mass movements concentrate in gneiss, suggesting lithology as an important preconditioning factor, although topography also plays a role. The inventory provides a basis for future studies on slope failure chronology, glacial influence on landscape evolution and susceptibility assessment.

papers.summary: Newly triggered landslides rarely carry immediate annotations, so cross-domain transferability determines the value of landslide mapping for emergency response and regional risk assessment. Vision foundation models have strengthened representational transfer, yet on unseen regions, events, and sources they still generate high-confidence false alarms. Terrain, material, and rainfall triggering can constrain such errors, but their supports are local, regional, and event-scale, so resampling onto a 10 m grid misaligns them with the segmentation decision unit and compounds the uncertain geographic context problem (UGCoP). We propose GeoPhysAdapter, which anchors on a frozen vision foundation model, restricts terrain, material, and triggering to dense spatial guidance, regional modulation, and event-timing forcing, and applies bounded adaptation at two decision units, the pixel and the candidate landslide body, reverting exactly to the visual prediction where support is insufficient. On an event-isolated PILD dataset of four public sources, 55 global landslide events, and 7890 test samples, 70.3% of cross-domain false-positive mass lies in near-pure spurious bodies of median equivalent diameter 207 m, matching coarse-prior support rather than the pixel. Pixel-level adaptation removes a net 507,817 erroneous pixels, reducing error by 7.76%, whereas raising the decision unit to the candidate body, under identical samples, anchor, and baseline, increases error reduction to 23.99% and improves IoU by a relative 14.2%. The gain decreases monotonically with terrain displacement, exceeds a strong optical control of spectral change and visual confidence alone by 0.019 IoU, remains positive across five vision anchors, and survives a pre-registered re-execution with a 20.61% error reduction. papers.title: Synergistic effects of climatic drivers and anthropogenic land degradation on cascading geomorphic hazards in Iran
papers.summary: Environmental hazard adaptation frameworks have predominantly focused on susceptibility to isolated hazards, often overlooking the complex dynamics of cascading land degradation. This study assessed the synergistic impacts of anthropogenic and climatic drivers on cascading geomorphic hazards in Iran. Our framework integrated land degradation models (MEDALUS and RUSLE) with downscaled outputs from 23 General Circulation Models. We introduced the Dust Hotspot Severity Index (DHSI) utilizing a multi-threshold spatial intersection of Aerosol Optical Depth anomalies. Our analysis revealed hydro-aeolian telecoupling, in which upstream hydrological alterations drive downstream aeolian dynamics. Severe upstream soil erosion and the expansion of hydrological infrastructure have reduced environmental flows to downstream wetlands, triggering neo-playa formation. The subsequent accumulation of erodible sediments transforms desiccated wetland and lake beds- such as Lakes Urmia and Hamun- into hyper-productive dust sources (DHSI > 20%). Copula-based ensemble projections under the SSP2-4.5 scenario for the near-future period (2026–2050) indicate that desertification and water erosion rates will increase by 17.53% and 15.30%, respectively. The spatial extent of moderate-to-severe cascading hazard potential (encompassing desertification, water erosion, and dust emissions) is projected to expand from a historical baseline of 45.30% to 58.60%. These findings demonstrate how the convergence of unsustainable resource management and climatic drivers pushes arid landscapes toward cascading multi-hazard regimes.

This paper assesses physical climate risks to Pertamina operational assets across upstream exploration and production (E&P), refinery, and retail and distribution business units located in Southern Sumatra, Western Java, and Central Sulawesi. The scope focuses on identifying climate drivers and hazards, including flood, coastal inundation, landslide, maritime extreme weather, and lightning, under baseline and projection periods to support risk-informed adaptation and resilience planning for diverse energy infrastructure. The assessment integrates science-based climate analysis, hazard mapping, and Health, Safety, Security, and Environment (HSSE) risk evaluation. Historical climate data (1983–2011) and future projections (2031–2060) were downscaled to establish atmospheric and marine climate baselines for Southern Sumatra, Western Java, and Central Sulawesi. Probabilistic models were applied to map flood, coastal inundation, landslide, maritime extreme weather, and lightning hazards. Asset exposure from upstream E&P, refinery, and retail and distribution facilities was overlaid with hazard zones, followed by risk scoring using Pertamina probability-impact criteria and Risk Priority Number (RPN). Adaptation options were formulated through the PDCA-based risk management process. The results show distinct physical climate risk characteristics across business units and regions. In Southern Sumatra, upstream E&P assets are primarily exposed to flood, landslide, and lightning hazards, reflecting inland topography and increasing extreme rainfall intensity. Refinery and retail and distribution facilities in Western Java demonstrate elevated risk from coastal inundation and maritime extreme weather due to low elevation and proximity to the northern Java coastline. papers.summary: Coastal caves developed in weak and heterogeneous cliffs constitute complex geomechanical systems in which lithological variability, structural discontinuities, groundwater seepage and marine erosion interact. Their stability assessment is particularly challenging in urbanised coastal and touristic attractive environments, where local failures may affect infrastructure and public safety. This study presents an integrated assessment of a natural cave system in the coastal cliffs of Las Grutas, Río Negro, Argentina. Field observations, structural mapping, geomechanical characterisation and UAV-based three-dimensional reconstruction were combined with empirical classifications, analytical roof-stability methods, and two- and three-dimensional hydro-mechanical numerical modelling. Parameter uncertainty was further explored through probabilistic sensitivity analyses. The results show that the different approaches provide complementary rather than directly interchangeable information. Empirical methods identify sectors with high geomechanical susceptibility, whereas the analytical assessment clarifies the roof-failure mechanisms associated with cavity geometry and stratification. Numerical modelling highlights the stabilising influence of three-dimensional stress redistribution while showing that groundwater flow and discontinuities control the localisation of deformation and the development of potential failure zones. The analyses also indicate that groundwater conditions exert a major influence on the calculated stability margins. Overall, the cliff system remains globally stable under the steady-state hydraulic and monotonic loading conditions considered, although local instability and progressive degradation may develop where basal weakening, seepage and unfavourable discontinuities interact. The study aims to describe and analyze the representation of ecological issues based on the tropes of pollution, wilderness, apocalypse, and animals, in order to deconstruct anthropocentric perspectives in literature. papers.title: DS-InSAR combined with dual-attention enhanced CNN-BiGRU for deformation prediction of typical landslides in the Jinsha River Basin
papers.summary: Accurate prediction of step-like abrupt landslide deformation is critical for disaster early warning but remains hindered by the over-smoothing bias of conventional models. This study proposes an end-to-end prediction framework integrating Distributed Scatterer InSAR (DS-InSAR) monitoring data with a dual-attention enhanced CNN-BiGRU network. Two architectures—direct-output and Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq)—were validated on the Guoba Landslide, a large landslide in the Jinsha River Basin. The dual attention mechanism adaptively isolates critical precursor features, enhancing both precision and interpretability. A global evaluation across all measurement points delineates their domains of applicability. The direct-output DA-CNN-BiGRU acts as a robust spatial filter, achieving a global R2 of 0.92 for ubiquitous continuous creep. Conversely, the Seq2Seq-DA-CNN-BiGRU is specifically optimised to mitigate this over-smoothing bias and capture severe step-like deformations, achieving an R2 of 0.636 at a representative critical point where baselines fail. Across representative kinematic points, it reduces average RMSE and MAE by 24.02% and 30.04%, respectively, compared to standard CNN-BiGRU. This study provides a targeted, interpretable early-warning scheme for complex landslides in high-altitude canyon regions.

Coupled influence of particle shape and basal configuration on rheology of granular media impacting against slit dam
papers.summary: Particle shape and basal boundary conditions play a crucial role in determining mobility, deposition, and impact response of granular flows; yet their coupled influence remains largely unexplored. To this end, we investigate rheology of dry granular media interacting with slit dam within a 3D discrete element setting with varying grain shapes and basal configurations. Besides spherical particles, we consider Platonic solids, viz., dodecahedron, octahedron, and tetrahedron, to explicitly isolate influence of particle morphological features, e.g., sphericity ( ψ ), as these shapes possess identical convexity and aspect ratio while differing primarily in various sphericity measures. Furthermore, we vary basal slip using plane smooth (PS), plane rough (PR), and undulated rough (UR) basal configurations. Comprehensive examination of flow kinematics, kinetics, and grain-scale signatures reveals that decreasing ψ suppresses flow mobility through enhanced particle interlocking and restricted rotation, thereby increasing residual force on barrier. With increasing basal roughness from PS to PR followed by UR, basal slip reduced, accompanied by energy dissipation. Analyses of granular temperature, shear rate, coordination number, force-chain evolution, and fabric anisotropy reveal micromechanical origins of observed macroscopic responses. Additionally, dynamic pressure coefficient ( k d ) scales with Froude number, which varies with ψ for different basal configurations via its control on flow velocity and depth, a relationship developed herein across sphericity measures. Interestingly, k d exhibits maximum value for UR configuration despite exhibiting lowest peak impact force resulting from moderate flow depth and velocity. The micro -to– macro insights further aid in improving impact-force prediction, thereby promoting enhanced design of landslide mitigation structures.

papers.title: Assessing the probability of rainfall-induced landslides along the vulnerable slope-aligned transportation corridor in Darjeeling-Sikkim Himalayas
papers.summary: Shallow debris slides triggered by rainfall are widely distributed along the NH-10 in the Darjeeling–Sikkim Himalayan region, and most of them are reactive in nature. The Himalayan region is vulnerable to reactivated landslides due to extreme rainfall during the monsoon season. The occurrence of landslides largely depends on rainfall patterns. Therefore, the present study focuses on establishing the probability of landslide events P(A|B) with a certain amount of rainfall intensity (0 ≤ I <15, 15 ≤ I < 35, 35 ≤ I < 55, and I ≥ 55 mm/d) and predicting the expected number of landslide events and the number of landslides in different return periods. To achieve these objectives, a Bayes’ probabilistic approach and the Gumbel method have been employed. The pre-requisite data sets, such as rainfall information has been collected from India Meteorological Department (IMD) and tea garden adjacent to the highway, while landslides data have been gathered from Public Works Department (PWD) of National Highway Division-IX, previous research studies daily newspaper and field surveys for the last 15 years (from January, 2011 to December, 2025). During 8 years (2011–2018), the highway witnessed 666 landslides from 278 landslide events were used to calibrate the models. In that period, total 911 rainfall events have been identified from historical rainfall datasets. Whereas, 33 field-identified landslides that occurred between 2019 to 2025 were used to validate the proposed model. The conditional probability of landslide events for a given rainfall intensity and landslide return periods has been estimated using the Gumbel model along NH-10. In addition, similar estimates have been made for four major lithostratigraphic units that span overs the highway. The results indicate significant variations in landslide probability among lithostratigraphic units. papers.title: Slope stability analysis of a plateau lake under strong earthquake impacts: a case study of Lake Sarez, Tajikistan
papers.summary: Strong earthquakes and complex terrain have produced unstable slopes around Sarez Lake, Tajikistan, threatening the Usoi Dam, downstream ecosystems and residents. Using Sentinel-1 images (September 2022–September 2024), we mapped surface deformation with SBAS-InSAR, classified two-dimensional deformation and integrated GNSS–InSAR data to analyze seismic anomalies. We inverted the focal mechanism using the Okada model, identified deformation zones via K-means and applied random forest–SHAP to assess environmental factors’ relative contributions and responses. The results show that horizontal motion dominates regional deformation, while seismic activity significantly induces slope instability. Three-dimensional deformation reveals slow lakeward movement of the Usoi Dam and slopes on both banks. The Mw 6.85 earthquake involved left-lateral strike-slip motion, with nearly E–W compression and N–S extension characterizing regional tectonic stress. Clustering places the Usoi Dam in a stable zone, with vertical subsidence dominating the left-bank slope and westward horizontal motion dominating the right-bank slope. Environmental statistics reveal marked topographic and geological differences among deformation zones. These findings provide quantitative evidence and remote-sensing support for deformation identification, environmental background analysis and safety risk assessment in alpine landslide-dammed lake regions.
