An integrated ArcGIS Python toolbox for SCS-CN event runoff estimation and flood screening in data-scarce Ethiopian basins
papers.summary: Flood early warning in data-scarce regions is constrained by sparse gauging and limited modelling capacity. We present an integrated ArcGIS Python toolbox automating SCS-CN event runoff estimation, from curve number generation and per-event antecedent moisture classification through to threshold calibration, evaluated in a semi-arid Ethiopian basin. From four quality-controlled stations, 587 rainfall events (2010–2023) were extracted; 98.6% occurred under dry antecedent conditions, corroborated by ERA5-Land soil moisture ( p < 0.001). Evaluation used nineteen documented flood windows from disaster databases and official reports, since discharge records are unavailable. Basin-mean runoff discriminated documented floods with AUC = 0.91 (95% CI 0.83–0.97; Cohen’s d = 2.6), rising to 0.95 for the eleven events triggered within the gauged area. A calibrated 1.25 mm runoff threshold detected thirteen of sixteen floods with approximately 62% fewer false alarms than the regional 30 mm rainfall criterion at equal detection, confirmed out-of-sample by temporal hold-out. Discrimination proved robust to the initial abstraction ratio and ± 10% curve number bias, whereas absolute thresholds were not, making local calibration essential. Limited gauge coverage and a small documented-event sample are acknowledged limitations, quantified via satellite-precipitation comparison and bootstrap intervals. The toolbox provides a transparent, reproducible flood-screening framework for data-scarce semi-arid basins.

papers.title: Integrated Earthquake-Induced Stability Assessment of Lam Chae Earth Dam using Sentinel-1 DInSAR and Field Instrumentation
papers.summary: The Mw 7.7 Myanmar earthquake of 28 March 2025 generated ground shaking across several regions of Thailand, including Nakhon Ratchasima Province, where the Lam Chae Earth Dam is located. Rapid and reliable assessment of dam stability following seismic events is essential for ensuring public safety and supporting reservoir operation. In this context, Sentinel-1 Differential Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (DInSAR) provides spatially continuous deformation measurements over large areas and complements conventional point-based field monitoring instruments. This study presents an integrated assessment of earthquake-induced dam stability using Sentinel-1 DInSAR together with field instrumentation, including inclinometers and piezometers. Sentinel-1 synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images acquired during the pre-seismic, co-seismic, and post-seismic periods were processed to derive line-of-sight (LOS) surface deformation and compared with in-situ monitoring data. The DInSAR analysis revealed a maximum cumulative LOS displacement ranging from approximately - 27 to - 30 mm during the co-seismic period, whereas inclinometer measurements indicated internal deformation ranging from - 1.258 to - 3.980 mm. Piezometer observations confirmed that pore-water pressure remained within the normal operating range throughout the monitoring period. Although DInSAR measurements are subject to uncertainties associated with atmospheric delay, temporal decorrelation, and vegetation-induced coherence loss, the observed deformation patterns were consistent with field measurements, providing complementary evidence for assessing dam behaviour. This study demonstrates the applicability of integrating satellite-based DInSAR with conventional geotechnical instrumentation for post-earthquake dam safety assessment in Thailand, where such integrated applications remain limited. papers.title: Peer Review Report For: Physical and Mechanical Characteristics of Soil as a Controlling Factor in Landslides in Curug Panjang Village, Cihuni Hamlet, Lebak, Banten: Analysis of Distribution, Normality, and Inter-parameter Relationships [version 2; peer review: 1 approved, 2 approved with reservations]
papers.summary: Background Landslide occurrence is strongly influenced by the physical and mechanical properties of subsurface soil; this study evaluates these properties in residual soil from Kampung Cihuni, Lebak Regency, as a controlling factor in landslides. Methods Thirty residual soil samples were collected at a depth of 0–1 m using a grid sampling method. Laboratory testing covered natural water content (w); specific gravity and unit weight, used to derive void ratio (e); the plasticity index (PI) from the Atterberg limits; and Unconsolidated Undrained (UU) triaxial testing for cohesion (c) and internal friction angle (φ). The distribution of each parameter was evaluated using histograms, Q-Q plots, and the Shapiro-Wilk normality test, while inter-parameter relationships were analysed using linear regression (R 2 ) and Spearman correlation (ρ). Results The Shapiro-Wilk test showed that cohesion (c) and void ratio (e) are normally distributed, whereas water content (w), PI, and friction angle (φ) are not. PI values for the plastic samples (n = 26) ranged from 13.8% to 86.7%, and φ ranged from 5.48° to 20.5°; the relationship between the two was weakly positive (R 2 = 0.151, p = 0.050; Spearman ρ = 0.244, p = 0.229). Cohesion ranged from 4.41–52.47 kPa but showed a very weak, non-significant relationship with water content (R 2 = 0.028, p = 0.376), as did void ratio with φ (R 2 = 0.089, p = 0.110). Conclusions Relationships among the physical and mechanical parameters were weak and mostly non-significant, so the reduction in soil shear strength cannot be explained by any single parameter alone. Because the UU triaxial test represents total-stress conditions, it cannot directly explain rainfall infiltration and pore-water pressure change as a landslide trigger, though it offers an initial picture of the residual soil’s engineering characteristics as a controlling factor in the area’s landslide susceptibility.

papers.title: A dynamic warning system for single-gully debris flows in Beijing mountain areas: model construction and performance verification
papers.summary: Debris flows in Beijing's mountainous areas feature sudden occurrence and high destructiveness, posing severe threats to residents' lives and property. Conventional early warning models based only on regional rainfall thresholds or static susceptibility suffer from low spatial resolution, high false alarm rates, and poor timeliness. This study develops a mechanism-inspired statistical dynamic early warning model for single-gully debris flows using multi-dimensional controlling factors and historical disaster data (2016–2022). The model establishes a composite geological index from four core indicators and a rainfall index using maximum hourly rainfall intensity and event-based cumulative rainfall. A power-law nonlinear coupling relationship is optimized via grid search, and a four-level graded warning system is constructed. Validated by three extreme rainfall events (2023–2025), the model achieves a Probability of Detection exceeding 97%, a false alarm rate below 5%, a critical success index above 0.80, and an average warning lead time of 1.2–1.5 hours. It has been implemented in the Beijing Geological Hazard Monitoring and Early Warning System for real-time operation. This work enables a shift from regional to refined single-gully warning, providing technical support for disaster mitigation and a transferable framework for similar urban mountainous regions worldwide.

papers.title: Study on three-dimensional deformation monitoring of railway slopes via synergistic integration of Beidou and InSAR
papers.summary: Abstract Remote-sensing-based slope stability monitoring is vital for railway safety. This study is grounded in the demands for high timeliness and multi-element monitoring of three-dimensional deformation of modern railway slopes. Aiming at the issue that existing technologies struggle to balance spatial and temporal resolution in the process of fusing and resolving three-dimensional deformation using the BeiDou Navigation Satellite System (BDS) and Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR), a point-surface hierarchical fusion strategy is proposed. After constructing a unified fused observation equation, spatial regularization constraints and local joint adjustment are introduced to balance spatiotemporal resolution from two levels. This ensures the consistency and reliability of 3D accuracy under the hierarchical strategy, while achieves constrained representation of the large-scale deformation trend and high-precision temporal evolution of the 3D deformation field. Building on the hierarchical fusion results, this paper proposes a 3D deformation risk classification method for railway slopes, enabling refined slope monitoring and early disaster warning with a feasible technical scheme. The effectiveness of the method is validated on typical slopes along the Shijiazhuang-Taiyuan Railway. The results indicated that (1) the average 3D deformation accuracy obtained by the point–surface hierarchical fusion strategy is superior to 10 mm, ensuring both accuracy balance and reliability under the hierarchical strategy while taking into account both spatial and temporal resolutions. (2) The proposed three-dimensional deformation risk classification method for slopes preliminarily verifies the feasibility of the hierarchical fusion strategy for 3D deformation monitoring of railway slopes considering both spatial and temporal resolutions.

papers.title: Analysis of stability influencing factors and failure mechanism of anti-dip rock slope under strong earthquake
papers.summary: Anti-dip rock slope is a common layered rock slope, and the failure mechanism of it under strong earthquake is not well studied. In order to analyze the stability and failure mode of anti-dip rock slope under strong earthquake, this paper investigates 60 typical failure cases of anti-dip rock slope, analyzes the effect of factors on slope stability, and summarizes the failure mode. Taking the Hongshiyan slope as an example, the dynamic response law of the slope under earthquake action was summarized, and the failure mechanism of the slope was studied. Finally, the sensitivity of each influencing factor was analyzed through orthogonal experiments. The results show that the failure mode of the anti-dip rock slope with hard rocks upper and soft rocks lower is the shear slip of the soft rock at the bottom and the tensile cracking and topplingfailure of the hard rock at the top. The influencing factors ranked in descending order of sensitivity are as follows: slope angle, seismic wave frequency, inclination, seismic wave amplitude, slope shape coefficient, and slope height. It is of great significance to study the failure mode of anti-dip rock slope under strong earthquake and evaluate its stability for slope disaster prevention and control in infrastructure engineering.

Geologically constrained dynamic evolution and early warning of urban resource-environment carrying capacity: a case study of Jinan, China
papers.summary: Urban resource environment carrying capacity (RECC) is increasingly challenged by nonlinear interactions among socioeconomic development, resource depletion, and geological environmental degradation. However, existing assessments often neglect the cumulative feedback effects of groundwater depletion and geological responses. This study develops a city-scale system dynamics (SD) model integrating six subsystems (population–economy, land, water resources, ecology, environment, and geological environment) to simulate RECC evolution in Jinan, China, during 2021–2031. A groundwater–geological feedback module is incorporated to explicitly represent the interactions among groundwater abstraction, groundwater depletion, land subsidence, and development constraints. A scenario-based early-warning framework is further developed to identify nonlinear degradation trajectories under alternative scenarios. Model validation indicates satisfactory performance, with R² and NSE values ranging from 0.87 to 0.97. Results reveal a transition from development-driven expansion to resource- and geo-environmental constraint regulation. Under the business-as-usual scenario, available water resources decline by 40%, the groundwater recovery index reaches − 0.35, land subsidence increases by 25%, and RECC declines by 28% by 2031. Water and geo-environmental constraints jointly contribute 71% of total RECC limitations, and a critical groundwater stress threshold is identified at approximately 1.15 (groundwater recovery index = − 0.15), beyond which degradation accelerates. Compared with business-as-usual, the resource-optimization scenario increases available water resources by 56%, reduces water pollution by 64% and land subsidence by 31%, delays high-level warnings by 2–3 years, and maintains 92% of per-capita GDP. These findings highlight the importance of groundwater–geological feedbacks for dynamic RECC assessment and sustainable urban planning.

papers.summary: Abstract. La Réunion is one of the French territories most exposed to natural risks. The island is exposed to seven major natural hazards: cyclones, floods, swells and tsunamis, landslides, earthquakes, wildfires, and volcanic eruptions. Numerous natural disasters have occurred on the island, as well as less significant natural events. This study presents a historical review of the direct impacts of natural events documented in departmental and national archives since human settlement on the island. Thus, in total 2,823 sources, referencing 1,266 events from 1655 to 2025 have been processed. The source's reliability is analyzed using a decision tree method. Based on the impacts, significance scores for each referenced event is established. An analysis of the evolution of impacts and mortality over time is conducted. A detailed geodatabase (HistoRiskRun) is created to capitalize information about natural hazards in La Réunion since its colonization. This database enhances documentation and understanding of past events and the evolution of risk management over time. This work provides elements to discuss the temporal evolution of impacts and mortalities associated with natural hazards and to relate these dynamics to the island’s geo-socio-historical context.

papers.title: geofm-landslide-benchmark: cross-model evaluation protocol and derived datasets for geospatial foundation models in landslide susceptibility

papers.summary: Reproducibility package for 'What survives an audit: evaluating geospatial foundation models for landslide susceptibility against a geomorphometric baseline' (in preparation for Earth Science Informatics). papers.title: LD-DETR: A Multi-Scale Landslide Detection and Segmentation Network for Complex Geological Environments
papers.summary: Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards. High-resolution remote sensing imagery provides an effective means for landslide detection and mapping, supporting geological hazard assessment and early warning. However, existing methods still face challenges in complex mountainous scenes with heterogeneous land cover and geological conditions. These challenges include irregular segmentation boundaries caused by diverse landslide shapes, small-scale detection difficulties due to background interference, and foreground–background class imbalance that hinders effective model optimization. To address these issues, we propose LD-DETR, a network for landslide detection and segmentation. An Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) module is integrated into the segmentation head to improve multi-scale feature representation, enabling better segmentation of landslides with varying spatial sizes. To alleviate class imbalance caused by the dominance of non-landslide pixels, a weighted Tversky Loss is introduced to improve the learning of hard samples. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is further combined with orientation-aware data augmentation to enable parameter-efficient adaptation, reducing the proportion of trainable parameters of LD-DETR to 41.07% while keeping the pre-trained backbone parameters frozen. Experiments on the Bijie and Luding Landslide Dataset (BLLD) demonstrate that LD-DETR is competitive with the baseline model and several YOLO-based approaches. The proposed method achieves an F1-score of 95.18% and a Recall of 95%, while the segmentation task reaches an mAP of 59.28%, slightly higher than the RF-DETR baseline. Furthermore, a limited-sample adaptation experiment on the Jiuzhai landslide dataset demonstrates the transferability of the proposed method across different geographic regions. These results indicate that the proposed framework provides competitive landslide detection and segmentation performance and offers an approach for fine-grained landslide

papers.title: A pseudo-three-dimensional work-balance correction for sidewall friction effects in centrifuge slope models
papers.summary: Abstract Centrifuge model tests are widely used to investigate slope stability; however, frictional interactions between the sliding mass and rigid container sidewalls introduce boundary effects that compromise similitude with ideal plane-strain prototypes. These effects can lead to an apparent increase in the stability of finite-width models relative to the corresponding plane-strain reference. In this paper, a pseudo-three-dimensional work-balance correction based on a classical plane-strain upper-bound mechanism is developed by introducing an additional out-of-plane sidewall-friction work-rate term evaluated from an assumed lateral normal-stress distribution into the global work rate balance. A random-search optimisation technique is employed to identify the critical failure surface geometry and the corresponding stability factor. The proposed formulation is checked against the classical plane-strain upper-bound solution and further compared with published centrifuge test data. Across the reported configurations, the calculated and measured critical acceleration scale factors show the same decreasing trends with increasing model height and slope inclination, although substantial differences remain for individual cases. A parametric study reveals that sidewall friction significantly increases the apparent stability factor at low width-to-height ratios, but this discrepancy diminishes rapidly as the ratio increases. For the representative cases examined at β = 60°, the sidewall friction angle and width-to-height ratio exert larger influences on the sidewall-induced relative deviation than the soil internal friction angle, while the influence of the soil internal friction angle is retained explicitly in the broader reference charts and tables. Reference charts and tables are further developed to quantify the width-dependent deviation for selected parameter combinations and relative-deviation thresholds. papers.title: Integrating earth observation and machine learning for forest fire risk assessment in Rasuwa district, Nepal
papers.summary: The complex terrain and increasing forest fire incidents in recent years make high-mountain environments vulnerable to forest fires, posing a threat to ecological and economic well-being. However, research related to forest fires remains limited in the mountain region. The study aimed to assess the forest fire risk by integrating eleven predictive layers (biophysical, topographical, climatic, and anthropogenic factors) and a Random Forest (RF) model in Rasuwa, a mountainous district of Nepal. However, the precipitation factor was excluded due to multicollinearity concerns. The model was validated using Area Under the Curve (AUC) and True Skill Statistics (TSS). With an AUC of 0.9 and TSS of 0.67, the model shows strong predictive performance and high reliability of the generated fire risk map. The most significant factors in the model’s ability to predict the forest fire risk were elevation, temperature, Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), and proximity to settlements. The study shows that 29.66% of Rasuwa district’s forest is at fire risk, with the highest risk in Kalika Rural Municipality (53.7%). In the study area, approximately 30% of fire incidents occurred at elevations above 3000 m. The results can assist the concerned stakeholders and authorities in developing effective forest management plans by prioritizing identified high-risk areas for early warning systems and fuel management.

papers.title: Uso de técnicas edafológicas en el estudio de condiciones ambientales antiguas y de cultivos indígenas en el Ecoparque Golondrinas, Andes Colombianos
papers.summary: The Golondrinas archaeological site is in the Colombian inter-Andean Aburrá Valley hillslopes (2,000 m a.s.l). The initial archaeological assessment presented here included field observations, archaeological survey, soil chemistry, palynology, and micromorphological analyses in five locations, to identify a representative site. The complete pedostratigraphic sequence was analyzed to characterize depositional and post-depositional processes and to evaluate the effects of pedoturbation, pedogenesis, and anthropogenic features in relation to paleohydrological information. The archaeological record was assessed through a soil profile representative of the Golondrinas site (3,800 m2) described at microscale. The results provide a basis for testing hypotheses and proposing interpretations about past ecological conditions and historical land use dynamics at the study site. The findings and soil analyses suggest a history of land use that may have been associated with relatively high biological activity and high organic carbon content under hydromorphic conditions, as well as with alternating phases of agricultural activity and natural forest cover in the past. The study also identifies the presence of significant surface water flows and episodes of landslide activity associated with the site's geomorphological setting, which may have influenced both historical and contemporary land-use patterns.

papers.title: Indian Knowledge Systems for Climate-Resilient Highways and Sustainable Infrastructure
papers.summary: India's roads are transporting food, medicines, cargo and chance through one of the world's most climate-vulnerable areas. Road infrastructure resilience is now regularly challenged each year with cloud bursts and landslides in the hills and interior, floods in the coastal area, floods and cyclones in the Indo-Gangetic plains, and prolonged heat waves in the oceanic interiors. This book emphasises that both modern engineering and the wisdom of Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS) gathered over centuries, need to be applied to the transport sector in the context of climate change, in an evidence-based and respectful manner. Since times immemorial, repair and maintenance of stepwells, tanks, ponds and canals along with planting of trees and protection of sacred groves has been carried out by the Indian communities. They were not water war, but rather “water walk through” in terms of traditional ecological knowledge practices. Today they serve as real-life examples to inspire climate resilient highways and sustainable infrastructure, but only if they are not romanticised. There are seven chapters in one thread. Chapter 1 will introduce IKS for climate-resilient highways and map the traditional wisdom with highway functions. The following chapter (2) reviews traditional water harvesting and NbD approaches for drainage such as bioswales, ground water recharge and road draining. Examples of artificial intelligence and machine learning backed by remote sensing and digital twins and explainable AI to enable predictive maintenance, flood forecasting, landslide early warning system and intelligent transportation systems are presented in chapter 3. Sustainable pavements and circular economy materials are reviewed in Chapter 4 including reclaimed asphalt pavement, warm mix asphalt, low-carbon concrete and permeable pavements, as well as waste plastic roads. Chapter 5 addresses embodied carbon, operational carbon and low-carbon infrastructure, how they connect to the design of highway

Evidence of vertical soil hydraulic heterogeneity regulating hydrothermal simulations in Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau wetlands
papers.summary: Abstract. Alpine wetlands on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau host vertically structured and highly contrasting pore systems that fundamentally shape land and atmosphere exchanges, yet their hydraulic expressions and process implications remain poorly quantified. This study provides the first process based and depth resolved characterization of these layered pore structures using soil physical analyses and laboratory evaporation experiments. The derived Clapp–Hornberger parameters reveal coherent hydraulic contrasts, with surface layers dominated by macropore connectivity and showing high θs and Ks and low b that promote rapid drainage and evaporation, mid layer domains with lower θs and Ks and larger b that enhance retention in finer pores, and deeper layers that act as stable and persistent storage reservoirs. These properties together generate a vertical regime of rapid near surface drainage, delayed mid layer release, and long lasting deep moisture storage. When implemented in Noah-MP, this hydraulic stratification systematically altered water and energy partitioning during wet and dry periods and showed that vertical hydraulic heterogeneity rather than a single layer parameterization governs the timing and magnitude of evaporation and heat fluxes. These findings provide the first quantitative evidence that pore scale structure regulates profile scale hydrothermal responses in Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau wetlands and establish a physically grounded basis for representing vertically heterogeneous hydraulic processes in land surface models.

papers.summary: Helical anchors represent a promising solution for anchor systems of floating offshore wind turbines, yet scour-induced changes to the seabed threaten anchor stability. The bearing capacity and failure mechanisms of helical anchors under such conditions have not been fully investigated. Finite element (FE) analyses examine scour geometry, anchor length, and soil heterogeneity (κ = kD/sum, where k is the undrained strength gradient, D is the shaft diameter, and sum is the surface strength). The results demonstrate that scour depth is the dominant factor governing bearing capacity, whereas scour width and slope angle have limited effects. Horizontal capacity is particularly sensitive to scour because the corresponding failure mechanism develops mainly within shallow soil. Increasing κ mitigates scour-induced capacity loss, with this effect being most pronounced as κ rises from 0 to 2, beyond which further increases yield diminishing benefit. Across different helical anchor embedment lengths, scour is shown to shift the critical embedment depth separating shallow and deep failure mechanisms, particularly under low soil heterogeneity. The effects of loading direction are further evaluated within the V-H loading space. Finally, predictive expressions are developed to capture the coupled effects of scour geometry, soil heterogeneity, and anchor length for engineering capacity assessment.

papers.title: Assessing the Effect of Landscape Restoration Interventions on Irish Potato Productivity in Nyabihu District: A Case of Selected Cooperatives
papers.summary: Land degradation and soil erosion threaten agricultural productivity in Rwanda’s Nyabihu District, particularly on steep slopes. This study assessed the effects of landscape restoration interventions on Irish potato productivity using a concurrent mixed-methods design. A sample of 177 smallholder farmers was selected from three cooperatives using Yamane’s formula, representing 55.3% of 320 households at a 95% confidence level and ±5% margin of error. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, t-tests, ANOVA, correlation, and multiple linear regression, while qualitative data from key informant interviews underwent thematic analysis. Results showed that 79.5% of farmers had adopted at least one restoration intervention: radical terraces, progressive terraces, or agroforestry. Adopters achieved an average yield of 19,654 kg/ha, compared with 10,054 kg/ha among non-adopters, nearly doubling productivity. Regression analysis revealed significant positive effects (p<0.001) from radical terraces (+4,733 kg/ha; 37.1%), agroforestry (+4,049 kg/ha; 33.6%), and progressive terraces (+3,873 kg/ha; 31.0%). Control variables were statistically insignificant, indicating strong independent effects of restoration interventions. Qualitative findings confirmed improved soil stability, moisture retention, and yields, but identified labour intensity, inadequate maintenance, and ageing farmers as constraints. The study recommends integrated terracing and agroforestry, expanded farmer field schools for the 47.9% adopting only one intervention, and comprehensive support during the first three years after terrace construction to advance NST2’s target of 50% crop production growth by 2029. Keywords: Nyabihu District, landscape restoration interventions, agricultural productivity, yield, and smallholder farmers.

Mapping groundwater-dependent vegetation in temperate climates on the example of Central Germany
papers.summary: Abstract Groundwater-dependent ecosystems are biodiversity hotspots that provide habitat for specialized species. The European Union (EU) Water Framework Directive (WFD) stresses the importance of identifying and protecting these ecosystems. So far, most studies focus on (semi-) arid regions, where groundwater use by ecosystems is both more prevalent and easier to detect. In this study, we adapt groundwater-dependent vegetation (GDV) mapping approaches developed for dry climates to temperate regions by replacing seasonal drought-based indicators with contrasts between dry and wet years. We implement this concept by integrating for the first time to our knowledge, ECOSTRESS evapotranspiration data with high-resolution remote sensing, regional geospatial data and botanical field observations. To test our framework, we trained and validated random forest models with eight predictor variables using 166 vegetation plots to identify GDV in Central Germany. Ground-truth GDV plots prefer cooler, wetter, nutrient-richer and more acidic to alkaline environments compared to non-GDV. The final model using a phreatophyte cover threshold of 25% representing GDV plots achieved a testing accuracy of 0.97, identifying 2067 km² of GDV. Currently, only 19% is protected under the EU WFD. The proposed mapping framework offers a solution for identifying GDV in temperate regions. The new GDV maps can contribute to managing groundwater resources and preserving biodiversity hotspots in regions facing increasing droughts, ultimately supporting the implementation of the EU WFD.

papers.summary: Volcanic islands are highly exposed to interacting geotechnical and hydrogeomorphological hazards, particularly where steep relief, intense rainfall, fractured volcanic rocks, and urban development coincide. This study analyzes the slope located along Avenida Sá Carneiro in central Funchal, Madeira Island, as an example of an urban coastal volcanic slope functioning under multi-hazard conditions. The study is based on literature analysis, field observations, and a sequential photographic inventory of existing protection measures. The results show that the analyzed slope should not be interpreted as a single retaining structure, but as a complex geological–hydrological–engineering–urban system. Its stability depends on the combined action of historical stone retaining walls, reinforced concrete elements, tunnel portals, drainage components, passive rockfall protection systems, terraced structures, vegetation, and local architectural solutions. The effectiveness of this system results from the spatial cooperation of many locally adapted measures rather than from one dominant stabilization method. The study also highlights the dual role of vegetation, which may support erosion control and near-surface stabilization, but may also obscure damage, seepage zones, and discontinuities. The findings emphasize that integrated slope management in densely urbanized volcanic island environments requires simultaneous consideration of water control, structural protection, maintenance, and landscape integration.:

papers.summary: Abstract. The Indo-Gangetic Basin (IGB) is a global hotspot for groundwater overexploitation. Previous studies have shown that groundwater levels initially rose due to enhanced recharge following the construction of irrigation canals, but subsequently declined as agricultural, municipal, and industrial abstractions intensified. However, the relative impacts of separate recharge and abstraction components (precipitation, canal leakage infiltration, irrigation return flow, and irrigation, municipal and industrial abstraction), remain unclear, as do the effects on groundwater-surface water interactions and environmental flows. This study therefore aims to quantify spatio-temporal changes in groundwater recharge and abstraction components over the past two centuries and assess how these changes have impacted groundwater–surface water interactions in the Upper Ganges–Yamuna interfluve in northern India. Groundwater model simulations indicate that canal water infiltration following canal construction after 1830 boosted recharge, but since the 1970s increased abstractions have lowered groundwater tables and reduced river exfiltration. Currently irrigation accounts for roughly 85 % of abstractions, with municipal (15 %) and industrial (< 1 %) uses accounting for much smaller shares. From around 2000, abstraction lowered groundwater tables to such an extent that local rivers likely shifted from draining to infiltrating conditions. As a result, groundwater–surface water interactions in local rivers may have fundamentally changed. This shift threatens environmental river flows, degrades surface water quality by limiting wastewater dilution, and harms groundwater quality where polluted river water infiltrates the aquifer, posing risks to both ecosystems and human health. Although both the Yamuna and the Ganges show reduced groundwater exfiltration, they are not (yet) infiltrating.

From Hydroclimatic Extremes to Recharge Planning: A Multi-Evidence Decision-Support Framework for the Multan-Lodhran Aquifer, Punjab, Pakistan
papers.summary: Groundwater depletion in the Multan-Lodhran aquifer is intensifying as pumping expands faster than replenishment. This study explicitly separates two evidence types: (i) published baseline endpoints, which are recalculated here for transparent growth and water-budget indicators, and (ii) analyses performed in the present manuscript, comprising area-weighted GRACE/GRACE-FO storage residuals (2002–2024), a five-model bias-corrected NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 precipitation ensemble, precipitation-extreme diagnostics, and GIS-based managed aquifer recharge (MAR) screening. From the published baseline, built-up land increased from 346 to 417 km2 between 2000 and 2023; municipal wells rose from 16 to 92 by 2020; the urban-central groundwater decline was about 0.57 m yr−1; and the recalculated recharge-to-abstraction ratio declined from 1.15 in 2006 to 0.72 in 2020 and 0.58 in the 2045 projection. The new GRACE residual analysis indicates persistent regional storage loss, but the GRACE/GRACE-FO mission gap and residual surface-water contributions preclude treating the full-record slope as a homogeneous groundwater-depletion rate; pre-gap Theil–Sen slopes were −0.42 and −0.48 cm yr−1 for pre- and post-monsoon conditions. Under far-future SSP5-8.5, annual precipitation increases by 21.88%, while winter precipitation declines and monsoon/post-monsoon rainfall and upper-tail extremes intensify. These climate results describe precipitation opportunity rather than simulated groundwater recharge. GIS screening identifies low-slope alluvial areas with surface-water access as candidate investigation zones, not validated MAR sites. The framework is therefore intended for planning: site-specific hydrogeology, source-water quality, infiltration performance, and monitoring must be demonstrated, and recharge measures must be implemented alongside abstraction control.

papers.summary: ABSTRACT The Wangdonggou ecological small watershed was taken as the research object. Based on the hourly monitoring data from 2020 to 2025, the multi-time-scale analysis framework of ‘hour-day-month-aggregation period’ was constructed, and the time-lag cross-correlation was adopted. The vertical lag response law of soil moisture at different depths to rainfall was systematically quantified. The core innovations are as follows: methodologically, the study achieved precise identification of the time lag between rainfall and soil water; in theory, the coupling relationship between ‘rainfall intensity, infiltration depth and lag response period’ has been quantitatively elucidated; in practice, a vegetation management plan has been proposed that prioritises herbs and shrubs, whilst requiring careful selection of tree species. The results indicate that the lag response period for the shallow layer (0–28 cm), middle layer (28–100 cm) and deep layer (100–255 cm) are 3–4 h, 23–24 h and 6–7 days, respectively; as rainfall intensity increases from light to heavy rain, the lag response period in the deep layer shortens from 9 to 3 days. This study provides a scientific basis for research into the ‘rainfall intensity-infiltration-root system’ coupling mechanisms on the Loess Plateau and for the construction of sustainable ecosystems.

Strength-permeability-disintegration evolution and microstructural coupling mechanisms of oil-contaminated silty sand at natural moisture content
papers.summary: Petroleum contamination can alter particle contacts and fluid distribution, thereby affecting the engineering behaviour of soil. This study investigates oil-contaminated silty sand under natural moisture conditions using unconfined compression, static-water disintegration, falling-head permeability, SEM–EDS, NMR, image analysis, and apparent water-droplet contact-angle tests. The UCS decreased continuously from 31.95 kPa at 0% oil content to 12.63 kPa at 12%, representing a 60.5% reduction. In contrast, resistance to static-water disintegration increased with oil content: the uncontaminated specimen disintegrated within approximately 50 s, whereas the 8% and 12% specimens remained largely intact after 24 h. Hydraulic conductivity and time to first water discharge showed non-monotonic responses, reaching measured maxima of 13.52 × 10 − 3 cm/s and 120 s, respectively, near 5% oil content. This response is regarded as an empirical turning feature under the present test conditions rather than a universal threshold. The microscopic results suggest changes in local particle-surface appearance, fluid-relaxation behaviour, visible interparticle spaces, and composite-surface wetting response. Overall, oil contamination weakened compressive resistance while delaying static-water disintegration, and the hydraulic response resulted from the combined effects of initial water entry, fluid distribution, local flow-path changes, and possible preferential flow.

papers.title: Load Transfer and Negative Skin Friction of Pile Foundations in Collapsible Loess: Field and Numerical Study
papers.summary: Abstract Wetting-induced collapse of loess can trigger significant negative skin friction (NSF) along pile shafts, leading to adverse effects on pile load transfer and bearing performance. Field static load tests were first conducted to investigate the load-transfer behavior of single piles under natural moisture conditions. Subsequently, in-situ immersion tests were performed using a combined wetting method involving an immersion pit and seepage holes to examine NSF development under wetting conditions. A three-dimensional numerical model was also established to interpret the pile‒soil load-transfer mechanism observed in the field tests and to conduct parametric analyses. The results indicate that the three test piles exhibit typical friction-pile behavior under natural moisture conditions. Wetting-induced staged collapse of the surrounding loess resulted in segmented NSF development and multiple neutral points along the pile shaft. Pre-wetting of the surrounding soil significantly intensified NSF development and altered the axial force distribution. The numerical simulation reasonably captured the general trends of load transfer and NSF evolution observed in the field tests. The findings provide insight into the mechanism of pile-soil interaction and NSF development in collapsible loess under wetting conditions.

papers.title: Assessing the Transferability of a Basin-Scale HEC-RAS Rain-on-Grid Model Across Independent Hurricane Events
papers.summary: Reliable simulation of hurricane-induced flooding is challenging because rainfall–runoff generation, river flow, and floodplain inundation interact across large basins. This study evaluated the cross-event transferability of a fully distributed, two-dimensional HEC-RAS Rain-on-Grid (RoG) model for the Tar–Pamlico River Basin in eastern North Carolina. The model integrates terrain, land cover, soil-infiltration properties, and gridded rainfall within a hydrodynamic framework. It was calibrated using Hurricane Matthew (2016) and was independently validated for Hurricane Florence (2018) using unchanged parameters. Performance was assessed against observed discharge, flood depth, and inundation extent. Across streamflow gages, calibration yielded Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) values of 0.73–0.99, coefficients of determination (R2) of 0.78–0.99, and ratios of root mean square error to observation standard deviation (RSR) of 0.10–0.51. Independent validation produced NSE values of 0.63–0.98, R2 values of 0.81–0.99, and RSR values of 0.15–0.60, indicating consistent performance despite differing hurricane rainfall and flood responses. The validated model was subsequently applied to a 500-year design storm to generate basin-scale flood-hazard information. The findings demonstrate that a calibrated basin-scale RoG model can retain useful predictive capability across independent hurricane events and support flood-hazard assessment and emergency planning in hurricane-prone river basins.

papers.title: Multidimensional spatiotemporal differentiation and driving mechanisms of soil erosion in a mountainous small watershed: an ST-TransUNet-R framework
papers.summary: Soil erosion threatens ecological security and water conservation in mountainous small watersheds. To improve pixel-level assessment under complex terrain and incomplete multi-source raster inputs, we developed ST-TransUNet-R, a deep-learning framework that integrates a ResNet-50 encoder, a Transformer module, a joint-validity mask, and masked mean squared error loss. The framework was applied to the Xikouwai Small Watershed upstream of the Miyun Reservoir for five assessment years between 2005 and 2020 and achieved R² = 0.87, RMSE = 2.08, MAE = 1.15, and PBIAS = − 3.13%. Multidimensional analysis showed that the 600–900 m elevation band contained 48.0% of the eroded area, whereas zones above 1100 m produced disproportionately high soil loss per unit area. Slopes > 35°, vegetation cover < 30%, unused land, and skeletal soils were consistently erosion-sensitive. SHAP analysis identified slope as the dominant predictor, followed by slope length and vegetation cover, indicating that terrain-controlled runoff concentration and surface protection jointly shaped spatial erosion heterogeneity. These findings provide a high-resolution basis for prioritizing erosion-control measures in mountainous water-source protection areas.

papers.title: Recharge Performance of Pond-Based Managed Aquifer Recharge in the Ramganga Basin
papers.summary: Groundwater underpins India's water and food security but faces growing stress from overexploitation and climate change. This study evaluates the hydrologic performance of small-scale, pond-based Managed Aquifer Recharge (MAR) interventions implemented under government development programs, in the context of India's plan to construct 14 million additional recharge structures. Focusing on the groundwater-stressed Ramganga basin, the study draws on three years of participatory monitoring of 23 recharge structures. Using topographic surveys, staff gauge installations, daily water-level records maintained by trained community members, and water-balance methods, 236 recharge events were captured and associated recharge volumes quantified. While the structures demonstrated utility in recharging groundwater, performance remained below potential with a consistent declining trend. The ratio of recharge volume to pond storage averaged 1.75 in 2023 but fell to ~0.8 in 2024-25, far below values of 5-12 reported in a nearby MAR pilot. Substantial variability was observed across structure types and seasons.Declining recharge rates were linked to siltation, inadequate maintenance, and hydrogeological constraints. Pond water availability (~140 days per season) was not the primary constraint; instead, low infiltration rates mostly below 40 mm day⁻¹ emerged as the dominant limiting factor. High evaporation losses (~28% of pond storage) further reduced effective recharge. These findings highlight the need for performance-based MAR planning, integration with watershed measures, regular operation and maintenance to manage siltation, context-specific designs particularly for multipurpose ponds and participatory monitoring to build local ownership and capacity.

papers.title: Soil Water Infiltration Under Bare Soil and Maize Straw: A Field Comparison of a Double-Ring Infiltrometer and a Rainfall Simulator
papers.summary: Soil water infiltration (SWI) is central to hydrology and erosion assessment, but the measurement method and surface condition may affect the rates obtained. We compared a double-ring infiltrometer (DRI) with a rainfall simulator (InfiAsper) on a Dystric Acrisol with a sandy clay loam A horizon, under bare tilled soil and under maize straw. InfiAsper applied five rainfall treatments of equal erosivity, combining intensities of 44.6–75.0 mm h−1 with durations of 106–38 min, on four to five plots per treatment and surface. DRI tests were carried out in the same fields (22 under bare soil, 13 under ground cover) and analysed as an independent group. We (i) determined the final infiltration rate (SIR_f), (ii) compared DRI with InfiAsper, and (iii) evaluated the Kostiakov–Lewis, Horton and Philip models. Under bare soil, InfiAsper means ranged from 21.6 to 37.7 mm h−1 and the DRI mean was 86 mm h−1. A planned contrast between DRI and the mean of the five InfiAsper treatments gave a DRI/InfiAsper ratio of 1.80 (95% CI 1.00–3.23; p = 0.049); with the 20 tests of at least 15 readings, it was 2.13 (1.22–3.71). Under ground cover, InfiAsper means ranged from 15.4 to 26.3 mm h−1 and the ratio was 0.65 (0.36–1.18) with all 13 tests and 1.73 (0.93–3.22) with the five tests that ran for at least 75 min. The ratio tended to be larger on bare soil than under ground cover, depending on which ground-cover tests were used. The intensity–duration combination did not significantly affect InfiAsper SIR_f. Horton fitted best for both methods and Philip worst. DRI thus gave roughly twice the final infiltration rate of rainfall simulation on bare soil, whereas no excess was found under ground cover.

papers.title: Preloaded and premoistened foundation that overlaps sabkha collapse treatment with construction evaluated by coupled infiltration and consolidation analysis
papers.summary: Conventional improvement methods applied to sabkha soil (collapse soil) are time-consuming, lengthening the project schedule. This paper presents a novel preliminary concept for a pre-loaded, pre-moistened shallow foundation engineered construction. A single-footing cast directly on dry sabkha incorporates a 3 × 3 array of vertical holes through which distilled water is introduced, advancing as a Green-Ampt wetting front and dissolving the evaporitic bonds before superstructure load application. The improvement phase overlaps temporally with foundation construction, thereby removing the improvement task from the critical path, as per the schedule overlap principle. A coupled boundary-value problem (Terzaghi consolidation) and a transient infiltration problem are developed to model consolidation and collapse settlement due to wetting, and they are verified against a plane-strain elastic stress analysis and a one-dimensional coupled hydro-mechanical Richards-BBM model. Results show that the innovative foundation mobilizes approximately 434 mm of collapse settlement within 12 days (reaching 509.6 mm total settlement including elastic deformation), accounting for close to 90% of the layer's 480 mm theoretical collapse potential (CP. H). Analytical (477 mm) and numerical BBM-LC (456 mm) models confirm near-complete collapse mobilization to superstructure placement. The schedule overlap reduces the pre-superstructure phase by 62% compared with traditional pre-wetting. This saving depends on the in-situ hydraulic conductivity. At 0.70 m sleeve spacing, the probability of completing wetting-collapse within the 14-day window is 0.62, so site-specific k v measurement and a pilot infiltration test are required.

papers.summary: Understanding soil water content dynamics under saline conditions remains a major challenge for effective soil and water management in agricultural systems. This study aimed to optimize the correction of soil water content measurements obtained from gypsum blocks under the combined effects of salinity and matric suction using Response Surface Methodology (RSM). Soil samples were collected from agricultural fields in Guangdong Province, China, representing three distinct soil textures: sandy loam, clay, and clay loam. These results demonstrate that RSM is an effective empirical approach for correcting gypsum block data under saline regimes, offering a practical solution for improving soil water content estimation and irrigation management in saline agricultural environments.

papers.title: Theory of Recession Based on Concepts from Percolation Theory
papers.summary: Abstract. Using the definition of recession as the decline in streamflow following a rainfall event peak and before the next peak (provided evapotranspiration may be neglected), recession defines the relationship between catchment storage and outflow. The present analysis addresses the limiting processes absent in existing recession analysis, which are nonetheless treatable in the language of percolation theory. This includes: a) a universal decline in hydraulic conductivity as the percolation threshold is approached, and b) a universal decline in accessible moisture content beyond the simple decline in overall moisture content. The process of addressing these two time-dependent phenomena generates the basic structure of recession response: 1) linear response for an average of multiple events, 2) the corresponding time frame variation, 3) the specific characteristics of its non-linear response, specifically, its convexity. The present approach results in an absolute value of the non-linearity that is still underestimated as compared to results published in the literature.

papers.summary: Nowadays, slopes forming transportation infrastructure are highly sensitive to hydraulic conditions such as rainfall, triggering negative impacts on ecosystems and road infrastructure. In this regard, this research analyzes the hydromechanical influence of a frequent rainfall intensity in northern Peru of 10 mm/h on the stability of slopes (T1, T2, and T3) under unsaturated conditions. For this purpose, simulations were performed using Plaxis 2D software, considering three slope geometries based on regulatory criteria for clayey gravel soils with fines content and groundwater table conditions. The input parameters for the soil were based on the Hardening Soil model, while the Van Genuchten model was used for flow analysis. The obtained results indicate that, within the analyzed section measured from the upper surface downward, maximum saturation reached a depth equivalent to 33% of the slope height for model T1, 11.8% for model T2, and 6.4% for model T3. In addition, the effective surface suction produced reductions lower than 3 kN/m² after 24 hours of continuous rainfall. Finally, the factor of safety was affected under the same scenario, decreasing by up to 59.11% for model T1, 49.2% for model T2, and 42.80% for model T3. It should be noted that the most significant transition toward instability occurred after 10 hours.

papers.summary: Abstract Urban ground collapse poses a severe threat to public safety, road operation and underground infrastructure in densely developed cities. This study investigates the hydro-mechanical failure mechanism of road collapse induced by coupled rainfall infiltration and pipeline leakage through physical model testing, finite element simulation and interpretable surrogate modelling. A validated numerical model incorporating saturation-dependent strength and stiffness degradation was used to generate 120 cases with different pipe burial depths, rainfall intensities and leakage pressures.The results indicate that collapse develops through shallow-soil pre-wetting, leakage-induced wetting-zone expansion, convergence of the upper and lower wetting fronts, and upward propagation of deformation. Leakage pressure is the dominant factor, contributing 86.42%, 87.79% and 92.77% to the variations in collapse depth, near-saturated zone area and wetting-front depth, respectively. Rainfall mainly dissipates matric suction and lowers the failure threshold, whereas burial depth regulates the wetting-front convergence and deformation-transfer path. GPR/Kriging achieved test-set (R 2 ) values of 0.997–0.998, while XGBoost-SHAP confirmed the mechanism of leakage-pressure domination, rainfall amplification and burial-depth regulation. Risk zoning further shows that increasing rainfall shifts high-risk conditions towards lower leakage pressures, particularly at intermediate burial depths. The proposed framework provides an efficient tool for identifying vulnerable pipeline sections and supporting targeted inspection and collapse prevention.

papers.summary: Recent advances in machine learning have improved rainfall-runoff prediction, yet most data-driven models remain difficult to interpret and do not explicitly enforce physical conservation laws. We present the Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM), a mass-conserving architecture based on the Mass-Conserving Perceptron (MCP). GCHM uses five storage states representing canopy interception, snow, soil moisture, groundwater, and streamflow generation. Constrained gates govern precipitation partitioning, evapotranspiration, infiltration, seepage, runoff, and baseflow while learning context-dependent process relationships. We evaluate GCHM across 50 CAMELS catchments spanning snowmelt-dominated, recent-rainfall, historical-rainfall, and arid regimes, using NOAA AORC meteorological forcing and remotely sensed vegetation and land-surface data. Performance is assessed using the Jawad-Kling-Gupta Efficiency (JKGE) metric, which accounts for stationary and non-stationary hydrologic behavior. We compare the full architecture with ablated variants and recurrent neural network benchmarks. GCHM reproduces streamflow dynamics across diverse hydroclimatic regimes, including arid catchments, while maintaining interpretable states and fluxes. Ablation experiments show that simplified architectures may perform adequately under wet conditions but struggle to represent flow persistence and recession during dry periods, when groundwater storage sustains low flows. Learned gates recover hydrologically plausible relationships governing snowmelt, runoff, seepage, and evapotranspiration. GCHM combines competitive predictive performance with mass conservation and interpretability, providing a foundation for hydrologic modeling and counterfactual analysis.

Internal Erosion in Glacial Tills: Mechanisms, Assessment, and the Potential of Transparent Soils—A Review
papers.summary: Internal erosion is a major threat to the long-term performance of embankment dams, yet its initiation and progression remain difficult to predict, particularly in broadly graded glacial tills. This review examines factors governing internal erosion susceptibility and integrates findings from empirical stability criteria, numerical modeling, hydro-mechanical investigations, and emerging transparent soil techniques. The review indicates that internal stability cannot be characterized solely by particle size distribution, but depends on the combined influence of soil structure, hydraulic loading, and stress conditions. Furthermore, suffusion emerges as a progressive hydro-mechanical process in which fine particle migration continuously modifies the soil structure and its hydraulic and mechanical response, thereby influencing the subsequent progression of erosion. Empirical criteria remain valuable screening tools, whereas numerical and experimental approaches provide complementary information on particle-scale and hydro-mechanical mechanisms. Transparent soils, formed by combining synthetic soil surrogates with refractive-index-matched pore fluids, provide optical access to internal processes and enable direct visualization of particle migration, clogging, and preferential flow. However, their application to glacial tills requires sufficient comparability of the physical, hydraulic, and mechanical characteristics governing internal erosion. Integrating these approaches may provide a more comprehensive framework for assessing suffusion in glacial till embankment dam cores.

For such rocks the leaching recipe (reagent, concentration, temperature, particle size, liquid-to-solid ratio and contact time) decides whether a deposit can be worked, and the pore structure of the rock sets how fast the solution reaches the metal. The recipe is still found by months of bench tests, without the pore structure. Lixa is a Python framework that joins the two. These numbers tune a multi-host kinetic model built from shrinking-core dissolution, Langmuir ion exchange and a reagent balance that includes carbonate and silicate gangue. A differential-evolution search then finds the recipe with the highest net value per tonne within reagent and effluent limits, and the same kinetics project it to a heap or to a well field, where the image permeability sets the injection pressure. Each numerical part was checked against an exact solution: lattice Boltzmann flow to 0.12 percent, column transport to 0.004 in relative concentration, kinetics to better than one part in a thousand. For a weathered-clay ore the search returns ammonium sulfate near 0.3 mol L⁻¹ at room temperature, the concentration used in practice, in 6 s. papers.summary: Wildfires in the Amazon have far-reaching climatic and ecological impacts, yet their predictability remains limited. Here we identify a large-scale atmospheric precursor of August–September Amazon wildfires: a June–July dipole mode of South Atlantic atmospheric rivers (ARs), characterized by suppressed AR activity in the north and enhanced activity in the south. This dipole is strongly linked to interannual variability in Amazon wildfire activity through land–atmosphere feedbacks associated with reduced precipitation and humidity, enhanced surface warming and solar radiation, and increased vegetation stress. We estimate that wildfire-related forest loss associated with this AR dipole mode accounts for approximately 26% of the observed interannual variability in total forest loss. Adding the South Atlantic AR dipole to predictors based on May–June sea surface temperature anomalies and June–July wildfire activity yields substantial predictive skill for August–September burned area (R² = 0.67). Climate model projections further indicate a future intensification of the South Atlantic AR dipole mode, implying increased wildfire-driven ecological degradation in the Amazon under continued warming. This study identifies a South Atlantic atmospheric river dipole as an early warning signal for Amazon wildfires, linking shifts in moisture transport to hotter, drier conditions and increased fire activity in the region.

The FE analysis results demonstrated that qult and cw values, and stiffness of the σ-s responses increased with increasing dw/B ratios until reaching the dc/B value. Beyond this threshold, the obtained values coincided with those corresponding to fully-dry condition. It was observed that groundwater position and the Dr of the soil significantly affected the geometry and dimension of the failure surface. Furthermore, new semi-empirical equations were proposed for predicting dc/B and cw values considering internal friction angle, dw/B, effective and saturated unit weight values, showing good agreement with the findings of the FE analyses.

papers.summary: Drainage has been widely adopted in pavement structures. Due to drainage, wetting and drying, subgrade soils may be subject to conditions ranging from saturation to partial saturation (unsaturated). Particularly, unsaturated soil exhibits matric suction in contrast to saturated soils. Matric suction can impact the mechanical response of subgrade soils. Thus, it is significant to clarify the effects of subgrade moisture variations on unsaturated soil behaviour and resulting pavement response. In this study, constant water content triaxial tests and the axis translation technique were employed to investigate the shear behaviour of unsaturated silty sand under single- and multistage loading. The multistage involved drying, wetting and free drainage stages. The shear behaviour and resilient response were demonstrated to reveal the effects of moisture variations in terms of shear strength and unloading modulus. The tests showed that peak shear strength generally demonstrated an increasing trend with a decrease in moisture content (about 20% at the confining pressure of 25 kPa), and the unloading modulus increased by about 126% at 25 kPa. Based on multi-layered elastic analysis, the effects of moisture variations on pavement response were also investigated as a representative. Maximum tensile/compressive strain, subgrade deformation and distress life were simulated. This study will help to extend the understanding of effects of dynamic moisture variations on unsaturated subgrade soils and support pavement drainage design.

papers.title: Modelling temperature-dependent hydraulic conductivity function of rooted soils
papers.summary: The performances of vegetated soil infrastructures (e.g., landfill covers, soil slopes and green roofs) are likely influenced by the temperature effects induced by decomposition of municipal solid waste, solar radiation, high air temperature and underground power cables. However, the dual effects of temperature and roots on soil hydraulic conductivity function (HCF) have remained poorly understood. In this study, temperature-controlled simplified evaporation experiments were conducted to measure soil water retention curves (SWRCs) and HCFs of rooted soils for temperature range between 24 and 54℃. Based on RT-SWRC model considering the physical occupancy of roots in pores (R) and temperature effects (T), a nonisothermal HCF model (i.e., RT-P model) was proposed by incorporating root-induced pore rearrangement (P). Furthermore, RT-P model was compared with Mualem’s model (i.e., RT-M model). Results indicated that saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ks) and unsaturated hydraulic conductivity (Ku) were increased by the roots. As the basis to develop RT-P HCF model, RT-SWRC accurately captured the temperature effects on SWRCs of both bare and rooted soils. For shrub-rooted soils in this study and grass-rooted soils from the literature, RT-P model provided a more accurate prediction for HCF than RT-M model under different temperatures, due to consideration of root-induced pore rearrangement.

papers.title: MF6PQC v1.0: coupling MODFLOW 6 and PhreeqcRM for variable-density reactive transport with evolving porosity and hydraulic conductivity
papers.summary: Abstract. Geochemical reactions can alter groundwater flow by changing solution density and porous-medium properties. Representing these feedbacks requires consistent exchange of chemical states and physical properties between reaction, flow, and transport calculations. We present MF6PQC v1.0, a Python framework coupling groundwater flow and transport in MODFLOW 6 with geochemical reactions in PhreeqcRM. MF6PQC updates solution density and converts mineral-volume changes into changes in porosity, hydraulic conductivity, and diffusion coefficients. It supports three schemes for coupling transport and reactions while retaining existing flow and geochemical model-building workflows. Comparisons with two established reactive transport models showed agreement in component transport, mineral reactions, and the evolution of porous-medium properties. An idealized evaporating salt-lake model reproduced density-driven circulation and evaporite zonation. In a heterogeneous evaporite-leaching aquifer, dissolution concentrated flow along preferential pathways, and density feedback strengthened this redistribution. MF6PQC provides configurable coupling schemes and property relationships for examining these interactions in groundwater reactive transport.

papers.summary: Abstract The pulsed nitrogen injection for methane displacement (PNI-MD) technology is a novel approach aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions and enhancing the extraction efficiency and utilization of methane from low-permeability coal seams. By conducting experiments with PNI-MD, the influence of nitrogen injection duration on the methane displacement effect and the coal deformation characteristics is analyzed. The gas flow state and the mechanism of blockage-unclogging and permeability-increasing are investigated, and the field application mode of PNI-MD technology in low-permeability coal seams is constructed. The results show that with the prolongation of nitrogen injection time, the methane displacement efficiency increases while the methane displacement ratio decreases. During the nitrogen injection stage (Stage A), the high-pressure nitrogen gradually affects the gas flow state within the coal and at the outlet end. The gas flow state within the coal in Cycle 1 is divided into five stages. High-pressure pulsed nitrogen generates periodic tensile and compressive stresses with strong alternating pressure, which promotes repeated changes in the mechanical properties of coal, and the cumulative effect of damage leads to fatigue deterioration of the coal. The blockage-unclogging and permeability-increasing effects throughout the entire process of PNI-MD are divided into four stages. Under varying nitrogen injection durations, the increase in coal permeability after the completion of PNI-MD ranges from 0.50% to 3.63%. The PNI-MD technology effectively leverages the dual role of multi-gas displacement for desorption and energy injection for changing coal properties to achieve the objectives of blockage-unclogging and permeability-increasing. The dominant mechanisms during the Stage A include carrying methane with charging energy (CCWCE), promoting methane desorption by sharing pressure (PCDBSP), enlarging pores with injecting energy (EPWIE), and expanding pores

Active earth pressure in unsaturated marginal backfills with stochastic tension cracks governed by the influence zone and transitional regime
papers.summary: Active earth pressure acting on retaining walls can be significantly affected by tension cracks that develop within unsaturated marginal backfills. Existing analytical approaches typically idealize these cracks as a continuous zone of uniform depth, neglecting their stochastic nature and the resulting variability in active thrust. This study presents a physics-informed stochastic framework for evaluating active thrust in unsaturated backfills containing spatially variable tension cracks. A physically admissible random field is developed in which crack depth is characterized by its mean, coefficient of variation, and correlation length, while crack location is governed by mean crack spacing. The generated crack field is integrated into a limit-equilibrium formulation incorporating suction stress and a log-spiral failure mechanism. Deterministic analyses first identify an Influence Zone (IZ) along the backfill surface where tension cracks affect active thrust. Monte Carlo simulations are then performed to quantify the influence of crack variability on the 95th percentile of the active earth pressure coefficient, K a,0.95 . Results reveal the existence of a Transitional Regime Domain (TRD) within the IZ where active thrust exhibits maximum sensitivity to crack variability and cracking-zone extent. The location and extent of the TRD depend on the statistical characteristics of the crack field, particularly mean crack spacing and depth variability. Among the stochastic parameters considered, the coefficient of variation of crack depth exerts the strongest influence on K a,0.95 , whereas correlation length has a comparatively minor effect over the conditions and autocorrelation models investigated. The proposed framework provides a practical tool for probabilistic assessment and risk-informed design of retaining walls with unsaturated cracked backfills.

papers.title: Machine learning estimation of unsaturated soil hydraulic conductivity functions using literature-derived pedotransfer functions and an interactive graphical user interface
papers.summary: Measurement of unsaturated soil hydraulic conductivity K ( h ), remains one of the most expensive and time-consuming procedures in geotechnical and hydrological engineering. This study presents a machine learning (ML) framework coupled with an interactive graphical user interface (GUI) for estimating unsaturated soil hydraulic properties from basic soil characterization data. The framework employs Random Forest and XGBoost ensemble algorithms to predict van Genuchten parameters ( θ r , θ s , α , n , K sat ) using readily available soil properties, including texture, bulk density, organic carbon, and particle size distribution. The models were trained and validated on a literature-derived synthetic dataset of 1500 soil samples generated using established empirical relationships from the ROSETTA, UNSODA, and Cosby databases. A 75/25 train-test split was used, with five-fold cross-validation performed on the training subset for hyperparameter optimization. Test-set performance yielded R 2 . Five-fold cross-validation yielded R 2 values of 0.766 for θ r , 0.937 for θ s , 0.995 for α , 0.984 for n , and 0.151 for log( K sat ). The predicted parameters were subsequently used to generate full Soil Water Retention Curves (SWRC) and unsaturated hydraulic conductivity curves K ( h ) via the Mualem-van Genuchten model. Comparison with classical empirical pedotransfer functions and multiple linear regression demonstrated comparable performance for K sat prediction while offering superior capabilities for full-curve generation. It is explicitly acknowledged that the reported accuracy reflects the models’ ability to reproduce synthetic reference targets rather than independent experimental observations. The accompanying interactive GUI enables real-time prediction, batch processing, and export of results for both research and practical applications in agriculture and environmental engineering.

A Fully Discrete, Mass-Conservative Adaptive Discontinuous Spectral-Element Method for the One-Dimensional Richards Equation in Mixed Form
papers.summary: We present and analyze a spatially and temporally adaptive high-order method for the one-dimensional Richards equation describing vertical water transport in unsaturated soil, with an emphasis on resolving sharp wetting fronts while satisfying a fully discrete water mass balance. The spatial discretization uses an arbitrary-order local discontinuous Galerkin spectral-element formulation with collocated Legendre-Gauss-Lobatto quadrature, and the time integration is based on a high-order Rosenbrock-Wanner method. We focus primarily on the mixed formulation of the Richards equation, which advances water content as the conserved variable while evaluating the nonlinear diffusion operator in terms of pressure head; the resulting fully discrete scheme satisfies the water mass balance in exact arithmetic, independent of spatial resolution and time step size, including under spatial and temporal adaptivity. In contrast, the pressure-head formulation advances pressure head through a nonlinear capacity function and satisfies the corresponding conservation identity only at the semi-discrete level. Numerical experiments examine convergence through spatial and temporal refinement studies, with mass conservation assessed under spatial and temporal adaptivity using the solver flux output method (SFOM). The SFOM results confirm machine-precision mass conservation for the mixed formulation, whereas the pressure-head formulation exhibits mass balance errors above roundoff. Moreover, in the temporal refinement studies, the mixed formulation yields more accurate solutions than the pressure-head formulation for a prescribed time step size. The combination of high-order accuracy, spatial and temporal adaptivity, and fully discrete mass conservation makes the proposed mixed-form discontinuous spectral-element method a promising approach for simulating unsaturated flow in next-generation land models.

papers.summary: Water is an important natural resource, but due to industrialization and agricultural activities, there has been contamination of water resources.With the rise in the global population and climatic changes, there has been a need for sustainable water use in agriculture.Thus, reuse of treated industrial wastewater for irrigation purposes has become imperative.The current study was carried out to determine the effect of treated paper board industry effluent in various concentrations mixed with rainwater on the growth, yield, and quality attributes of bitter gourd grown using soilless culture technique.In the study, there were five treatments consisting of rainwater irrigation (T₁), 25% effluent concentration (T₂), 50% effluent concentration (T₃), 75% effluent concentration (T₄), and 100% effluent concentration (T₅).All the treatments were replicated five times, and each received equal fertigation dose of 100:25:25 g N:P₂O₅: K₂O.Results obtained from observations such as vine length, nodes per plant, leaf area, leaf area index, vine dry weight, root dry weight, fruit dry weight, and total dry weight showed no significant difference between the treatments.Quality attributes of bitter gourd fruits also revealed minor variations, which were not statistically significant.This implies that treated paperboard industrial effluents may be used as an additional irrigation source for growing bitter gourd without any harm to the yield.Nonetheless, there is a need for further studies to determine proper effluent concentrations as well as their impact on crop production.

papers.title: Radiocarbon in dissolved inorganic carbon in unsaturated zone soil water of semi-arid western India
papers.summary: Abstract Estimating groundwater age is vital for water management, especially in semi-arid regions, where aquifers are the primary freshwater source. Radiocarbon ( 14 C) dating of dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) is widely used to estimate groundwater age, assuming DIC is derived mainly from modern soil CO 2 , while soil carbonate contributions are considered 14 C-dead. However, in semi-arid regions, soil carbonates contributing to DIC in unsaturated zone soil water (UZSW) may contain measurable 14 C activity. This can impart an apparent age which is different from that assumed in conventional correction models and thus needs to be properly accounted for in groundwater age estimations. Here, we measured 14 C and δ 13 C in DIC in UZSW, soil CO 2 , soil carbonates, and soil organic matter to identify DIC sources and assess their impact on groundwater dating. Results show that the ages of DIC in UZSW range from 90 to 2290 years, with an average of ∼1240 years in semi-arid western India. We estimated that ∼13% of DIC derives from soil carbonates with 14 C ages in the range of 3500–14,000 BP in this region. These findings suggest that 14 C-based groundwater age estimates, particularly for groundwater younger than 10,000 years, may be biased if the 14 C activity of soil carbonates are not adequately accounted for. Our study also highlights the analytical challenges associated with isolating DIC for 14 C measurements. Overall, our results underscore the importance of characterizing the 14 C signature of soil carbonates and incorporating it into groundwater dating frameworks to improve the reliability of groundwater age determinations.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are prevalent geological hazards in mountainous and hilly regions, posing significant threats to human lives, property, and infrastructure, especially when external factors such as heavy rainfall elevate the risk of occurrence. In recent years, the rapid development of remote sensing technology, geographic information system, and big data analytics has enabled the establishment of landslide databases and the refinement of landslide hazard assessment methodologies, opening new avenues for disaster prediction and prevention research. This study focuses on the probabilistic hazard assessment of rainfall-induced landslides, using the heavy rainfall event in Nanping City, Fujian, in 2019 as a case study. The absolute probability of landslide occurrence was quantified by integrating machine learning models with Bayesian probability theory. To analyze their contributions to landslide hazard, the study comprehensively considered nine key factors: elevation, slope angle, slope aspect, topographic wetness index, fault distance, rainfall amount, topographic position index, land cover, and stratum. The findings reveal that rainfall intensity is the primary trigger for landslides. However, the occurrence of landslides also depends on the combined influence of topography, geology, and human activities rather than rainfall alone. Building on these insights, this study extends the established landslide probability assessment model to a wider region. And simulating landslide occurrence probabilities under various rainfall scenarios. This approach confirms the strong correlation between rainfall and landslides while offering scientific support for emergency management and disaster warning systems. The research provides a robust foundation for disaster prevention and control in mountainous areas, infrastructure planning, and the development of emergency response systems, particularly by refining landslide prediction models that account for multiple factors.
